Banks may open simplified "small accounts" for calamity-displaced persons lacking identification documents and may waive or reduce fees/charges for affected customers for up to one year. Key requirements include mandatory board-approved policies, specific conduct and customer protection standards for digital lending arrangements, and detailed prudential conditions for project finance disbursement and monitoring. The Directions apply immediately upon issuance and establish regulatory safeguards to ensure orderly growth, financial stability, and protection of depositors' and borrowers' interests while encouraging innovation in credit products and delivery mechanisms.

# RBI Circular Summary: All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025

The RBI has issued mandatory Directions applicable to five AIFIs (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID) establishing a comprehensive framework for responsible lending conduct, requiring Board-approved policies on Fair Practices Code, grievance redressal mechanisms, and penal charges. Key requirements include full transparency in loan disclosures (processing fees, pre-payment charges, penalties, conversion charges), displaying "all-in cost" on websites, written communication of loan rejection reasons, and verification of applications within reasonable timeframes. AIFIs must ensure non-discriminatory charges, proper credit appraisal independent of collateral substitution, and implement grievance redressal mechanisms with dispute resolution at next higher levels, with periodic Board reviews of compliance and mechanism functioning.

RBI's 2026 Directions mandate commercial banks to implement the Basel III Standardised Approach for calculating risk-weighted assets and capital requirements for credit risk, effective April 1, 2027. The framework establishes specific risk weights for various exposure classes (sovereigns, corporates, retail, real estate, NPAs, etc.) and incorporates external credit ratings from eligible agencies for determining capital adequacy. Banks must comply with enhanced due diligence requirements, credit risk mitigation principles, and apply standardised methodology for securitisation exposures to ensure prudent and comparable risk assessment across the banking system.

Rural Co-operative Banks must become members of all RBI-registered Credit Information Companies (CICs) and report credit information using standardized Uniform Credit Reporting Format (UCRF) with membership fees capped at ₹10,000 one-time and ₹5,000 annually per CIC. The directions establish a comprehensive framework for credit information reporting, dissemination, data quality standards, customer grievance redressal, and compensation mechanisms to ensure confidentiality, security, and consumer protection. These directions came into immediate effect from November 28, 2025, and apply to all State and Central Co-operative Banks operating as rural credit institutions.

ai_summary: These RBI Directions, 2025, establish comprehensive regulatory framework for Local Area Banks' branch authorization and outlet operations, covering banking outlets, Business Facilitators/Correspondents, doorstep banking, and ATM/CDM deployment with strict governance requirements. LABs must obtain Board-approved policies for opening banking outlets, which must operate minimum four hours daily for five days weekly with proper signage, monitoring mechanisms, and grievance redressal systems. The Directions define various banking service delivery models including Administrative Offices, Back Offices, and specialized outlets, while mandating banks to report outlet information to RBI and ensure transparent operations with appropriate risk management, particularly for doorstep and correspondent-based banking services.

The RBI's 2025 Directions establish comprehensive guidelines for Small Finance Banks on classifying investments into four categories (HTM, AFS, FVTPL/HFT, and Associates/Joint Ventures), with specific requirements for initial recognition, subsequent measurement, and fair value determination based on market activity and security type. Banks must establish investment policy frameworks approved by their Boards, implement robust internal controls, maintain Investment Fluctuation Reserves, and follow prescribed income recognition and non-performing investment provisioning standards. These Directions, effective immediately, replace previous investment portfolio guidelines and require banks to comply with detailed operational, accounting, and reporting requirements while ensuring all investment activities remain permissible under existing statutory and regulatory frameworks.

# RBI KYC Directions for NBFCs - Summary

These Master Directions, effective from their RBI website publication, establish comprehensive Know Your Customer (KYC), Anti-Money Laundering (AML), and Countering Terrorist Financing (CFT) requirements for all Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) with customer interfaces, aligned with India's FATF commitments and the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002. The Directions cover customer acceptance policies, risk management, customer identification procedures, due diligence, record management, and reporting obligations to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India, with additional requirements for NBFC branches and subsidiaries operating abroad to comply with the more stringent of local or RBI regulations. Non-compliance frameworks and detailed procedural requirements across eleven chapters govern NBFCs' obligations to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing while maintaining financial system integrity.

The RBI has issued consolidated Master Directions mandating the implementation of Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) codes for all OTC transactions in government securities, money market instruments, foreign exchange, and derivatives markets, effective immediately, with LEI required from accredited Local Operating Units (LOUs) for all non-individual entities. Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI) implementation is mandated from January 1, 2027, for transaction tracking and transparency, with non-derivative FX transactions subject to LEI only when exceeding USD 1 million equivalent. Market participants, intermediaries, and settlement entities must capture and maintain LEI codes in their systems, with non-compliance preventing entities from undertaking transactions in RBI-regulated financial markets.

# RBI Amendment Directions Summary

Banks must complete the wilful defaulter classification process within six months of an account being classified as NPA, following the mechanism outlined in Paragraph 5 of the original Directions, contingent upon wilful default being identified during internal preliminary screening. This amendment aligns the wilful defaulter treatment framework with the updated Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions issued in 2026. The amendment becomes effective from April 1, 2027, providing commercial banks with a defined timeline for completing classification procedures.

The RBI Master Direction 2024 consolidates and supersedes previous regulations governing Commercial Paper (CP) and Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) with original maturity up to one year, establishing unified rules for eligible market participants effective April 01, 2024. The Direction defines key terms including eligible issuers (banks, AIFIs, body corporates, companies, co-operatives), settlement mechanisms (DvP), and market infrastructure requirements, while applying to all entities dealing in these money market instruments. This comprehensive regulatory framework replaces prior fragmented notifications and incorporates market feedback to modernize the CP and NCD market structure and operational requirements.

Small Finance Banks with 10 or more banking outlets as of March 31, 2025, must establish an Internal Ombudsman (IO) office to strengthen their grievance redress mechanism and enable apex-level review of customer complaints before rejection. The IO must be a retired or serving officer at General Manager rank or equivalent with relevant experience, and the directions come into force immediately, with specific compliance deadlines (June 30, 2026) for operational clauses. This framework aims to ensure faster and more meaningful resolution of customer complaints by creating an independent internal review authority within each qualifying bank.

This RBI amendment to the Local Area Banks Responsible Business Conduct Directions (effective July 1, 2026) adds provisions enabling banks to maintain essential banking services in calamity-affected areas through temporary premises, alternative ATM arrangements, and satellite/mobile banking facilities. The directions permit opening simplified accounts without full identification documents for disaster-displaced persons and allow banks discretionary authority to waive or reduce fees and charges for affected customers for up to one year. These measures aim to ensure financial inclusion and continuity of banking services in declared calamity zones while providing relief to impacted customers.

The RBI's Payments Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 consolidates regulatory instructions on customer service, fair conduct, and financial inclusion for payments banks into a unified framework applicable immediately upon issuance. The directions establish institutional frameworks, customer protection mechanisms, guidelines for payment and remittance services, and deposit account management, with detailed definitions distinguishing between bank-induced and customer-induced transactions. Payments banks must comply with these directions covering customer guidance, financial inclusion accessibility, responsible business practices, and settlement procedures, enforced under Sections 35A, 45ZC(3), and 45ZE(4) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

# RBI Master Directions Summary (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) 2025

The RBI has consolidated Basel III prudential guidelines covering four key areas: Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR) for derivative exposures, capital requirements for Central Counterparties (CCPs), minimum capital requirements for operational risk using Basel III Standardised Approach, and Interest Rate Risk in Banking Book (IRRBB) governance and measurement. These Directions apply to commercial banks (excluding SFBs, LABs, PBs, and RRBs) and establish comprehensive frameworks for computing exposures, stress testing, and risk assessment in alignment with latest Basel Committee standards. Implementation dates for these consolidated guidelines will be communicated separately by RBI, consolidating previously issued instructions on counterparty credit risk, CCP exposures, operational risk capital, and IRRBB management.

The directions mandate adherence to specified credit data reporting timelines and formats while establishing mechanisms for consumer access to credit information, grievance redressal through the RBI Ombudsman Scheme, and compensation frameworks for data-related damages. These requirements aim to enhance credit information standardisation, protect data confidentiality and security, and strengthen consumer safeguards in the credit reporting ecosystem for Local Area Banks.

# RBI Circular Summary: NBFC Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025

These directions establish a comprehensive framework for early identification, reporting, and time-bound resolution of stressed assets by NBFCs, with differentiated requirements for deposit-taking NBFCs and non-deposit-taking NBFCs with asset size of ₹500 crore or more versus smaller NBFCs. The directions cover resolution mechanisms including inter-creditor agreements, restructuring plans, asset classification norms, provisioning requirements, and special cases such as compromise settlements, technical write-offs, and government debt relief schemes. NBFCs must implement board-approved policies for stress management, maintain enhanced disclosures, and adhere to specified prudential norms including asset classification post-restructuring, income recognition standards, and regulatory exemptions from SEBI regulations for instruments acquired during restructuring.

Local Area Banks must maintain a Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) reported under Form A and a Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) reported under Form VIII, with SLR comprising approved securities including Government of India dated securities, Treasury Bills, and State Development Loans. The directions define aggregate deposits as demand and time deposits combined, require apportionment of savings bank accounts semi-annually based on minimum balance averages, and specify that only unencumbered SLR securities qualify except for those used as MSF collateral or acquired under RBI-LAF arrangements. Penalties apply for non-compliance with these reserve maintenance and reporting requirements, establishing a comprehensive regulatory framework for Local Area Banks' liquidity and reserve management.

This Master Direction establishes a penalty scheme for bank branches and Currency Chests to enforce compliance with customer service standards and operational guidelines related to currency management and the Clean Note Policy. Banks face penalties ranging from ₹50 per piece for note/coin shortages to ₹10,000 per violation for service deficiencies such as refusal to exchange soiled notes, denial of facilities to linked branches, or CCTV non-compliance, with enhanced penalties of up to ₹5 lakh for repeated violations within consecutive inspection cycles. The scheme applies to remittances to RBI, currency chest operations, ATM replenishment, and exchange of notes and coins, with immediate recovery and penalty imposition upon detection of irregularities.

The RBI announced an auction of ₹32,000 crore in Government of India dated securities on May 15, 2026, comprising ₹21,000 crore of 6.36% GS 2031 and ₹11,000 crore of new GS 2066, with settlement on May 18, 2026. Bids will be submitted electronically through e-Kuber system using multiple price method, with non-competitive bids (10:30-11:00 a.m.) and competitive bids (10:30-11:30 a.m.) accepted separately, and results announced the same day. Up to 5% of notified amount per security will be allotted to non-competitive bidders (individuals and institutions), with facility available through Retail Direct portal, while Primary Dealers can underwrite additional amounts from 9:00-9:30 a.m.

# RBI Circular Summary: Rural Co-operative Banks – Debit Cards (2025)

The RBI has issued mandatory directions applicable to all Rural Co-operative Banks (State and Central Co-operative Banks) establishing comprehensive regulations for debit card issuance and conduct, effective immediately. Banks must formulate Board-approved policies covering debit card issuance, co-branding arrangements, card blocking procedures, grievance redressal, and compensation frameworks, with debit cards limited to Savings Bank and Current Account holders only. The directions define key terms including cardholder, co-branded cards, loyalty programs, and form factors while requiring compliance with existing RBI prudential, payment, and cyber security directives, though prior RBI approval for issuing debit cards is not necessary.

The RBI's Payments Banks – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025 establishes comprehensive regulatory requirements for payments banks covering deposit acceptance, governance, compliance, and operational standards under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Key mandates include board-approved policies for lending to employees, donations, staff certifications, mandatory leave requirements, and property valuation, along with strict prohibitions on high-risk activities such as loans, prize chit schemes, and lottery ticket sales. The directions also mandate implementation of KYC updation campaigns, FATCA compliance, CERSAI registration for security interests, and depositor education fund contributions, ensuring robust regulatory oversight and consumer protection in the payments banking sector.

This Master Direction establishes a penalty scheme for bank branches and currency chests failing to meet customer service standards under Clean Note Policy objectives, with penalties ranging from ₹50 per note piece for shortages to ₹10,000 for operational guideline violations. Key penalty triggers include: shortages in soiled note remittances, counterfeit/mutilated notes detection, CCTV non-compliance, failure to use Note Sorting Machines, and denial of coin exchange or note replacement services to customers. Penalties are levied immediately upon detection and escalate for repeat offences, with enhanced charges of ₹10,000 for recurrence within consecutive inspection cycles.

These Directions establish prudential norms for dividend declaration by 11 categories of NBFCs and housing finance companies, requiring Board oversight of supervisory findings, audit qualifications, and long-term growth plans before declaring dividends. NBFCs must meet specified minimum prudential requirements including CRAR, ANW, and NPA ratio thresholds to be eligible for dividend declaration, with dividend payout ratios capped at defined limits. The Directions come into effect immediately and apply to all layers of the specified NBFC categories, with mandatory reporting through designated formats, superseding previous dividend declaration guidelines.

The RBI issued the Rural Cooperative Banks – Credit Risk Management Second Amendment Directions, 2026, adding Chapter IIA on Credit Risk Evaluation, which mandates that rural cooperative banks incorporate potential impacts of calamities on borrowers into their credit assessment processes. The amendment becomes effective July 1, 2026, and is issued under sections 20, 21, 35A, and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. This requirement aims to strengthen credit risk management by ensuring banks adequately evaluate borrower vulnerability to natural disasters and other calamitous events during the lending process.

# RBI Small Finance Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025

These Master Directions consolidate RBI's regulatory instructions on customer service and responsible business conduct specifically for Small Finance Banks, covering institutional frameworks, customer guidance, financial inclusion, responsible lending, and deposit account management. The Directions establish comprehensive requirements across ten chapters including deposit account handling, safe deposit locker procedures, payment services, and claims settlement, with detailed annexes providing standardized formats and forms for implementation. Small Finance Banks must immediately comply with these Directions, which supersede previous scattered instructions and provide a unified regulatory framework to enhance customer service standards and ensure fair dealing in the sector.

The RBI's 2025 Know Your Customer Directions establish mandatory AML/CFT compliance requirements for five All-India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID) to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing in alignment with FATF standards and India's legal framework. AIFIs must implement comprehensive customer acceptance policies, customer identification procedures, enhanced due diligence measures, and ongoing transaction monitoring, with applicable provisions extending to their foreign branches and subsidiaries where not contradictory to local laws. The directions impose strict record management, beneficial owner identification, and reporting obligations to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU-India), with stricter standards applied when host country regulations diverge, effective immediately from November 28, 2025.

The RBI has amended the Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025 by adding "AgriSURE - Agri Fund for Start Ups & Rural Enterprises" to Annex XII, effective immediately from April 27, 2026. This amendment, issued under sections 26A and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, expands the scope of eligible funds or schemes available to Local Area Banks. The modification aims to facilitate agricultural entrepreneurship and rural enterprise development through designated funding mechanisms.

The RBI amendment directions modify investment portfolio classification and valuation requirements for commercial banks, introducing definitions aligned with the Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions 2026, including amortised cost, effective interest rate (EIR), expected credit loss (ECL), loss allowance, and stage classifications. Banks must measure investments at fair value on initial recognition, with HTM and AFS classifications including transaction costs, while zero-coupon instruments' carrying costs are adjusted using the effective interest rate method or prevailing acquisition rates. These amendments establish harmonised accounting standards for financial asset recognition, measurement, and provisioning across banks' investment portfolios, ensuring consistency with RBI's updated prudential framework.

# RBI Circular Summary: Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend Directions, 2026

These Directions, effective from FY 2026-27, establish prudential norms for Local Area Banks' dividend declarations, requiring board oversight of NPA trends, audit findings, capital compliance, and growth plans before approval. LABs must maintain regulatory capital compliance both before and after dividend payment, have positive adjusted PAT (after 50% NNA deduction), and are not subject to RBI restrictions, with dividend payouts capped at 80% of adjusted PAT on a tiered CRAR basis ranging from 0% at ≤9% CRAR to 100% at >21% CRAR. Exceptional/extraordinary profits and profits related to audit-qualified statements are ineligible for distribution, with non-compliance attracting penal consequences.

The RBI Amendment Directions, 2026 modifies the Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) Financial Services Directions by adding "AgriSURE - Agri Fund for Start Ups & Rural Enterprises" to Annex I, expanding the scope of financial services that RRBs are authorized to undertake. This amendment, issued under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, came into force with immediate effect as of April 27, 2026, enabling RRBs to support agricultural entrepreneurship and rural enterprise development. The directive aims to strengthen RRBs' role in promoting agricultural innovation and rural economic growth by facilitating access to finance for agri-startups and rural enterprises.

Banks must examine all banknotes for authenticity using machines before crediting accounts or dispensing cash, and must impound any counterfeit notes with a standardized stamp in a separate register without returning them to customers or destroying them. Detected counterfeit notes must be reported to police monthly (consolidated report for up to 4 pieces) or immediately via FIR (for 5 or more pieces), with acknowledgement receipts issued to tenderers and copies forwarded to the Forged Note Vigilance Cell. Banks must establish a Forged Notes Vigilance Cell at head office, designate nodal officers, provide staff training on detection methods, and report monthly data to RBI and other authorities, with willful failure to impound counterfeit notes constituting grounds for penalties as involvement in circulation.

These Directions establish prudential capital adequacy norms for five All India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, and NaBFID), effective immediately, requiring compliance with regulatory capital composition standards including Common Equity Tier 1, Additional Tier 1, and Tier 2 capital requirements. AIFIs must implement Board-approved policies for Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), manage risk-weighted assets across credit, market, and operational risks, and maintain minimum leverage ratios as specified in the framework. The Directions mandate comprehensive supervisory review, market discipline through Pillar 3 disclosures, and transitional arrangements for compliance, ensuring these institutions maintain adequate capital buffers to absorb losses and support their developmental lending mandates.

These Directions, effective immediately, establish comprehensive risk management requirements for Local Area Banks' material IT outsourcing arrangements, covering governance, service provider evaluation, security, business continuity, and specific provisions for group outsourcing, offshore arrangements, and cloud services. Existing IT outsourcing agreements must comply with these requirements by April 10, 2026 or at renewal, whichever is earlier, while new agreements must comply from inception. The Directions apply to core IT services including infrastructure management, network security, application development, data centre operations, cloud computing, and managed security services, but exclude corporate internet banking from regulated entities, external audit services, and SMS gateways.

# Summary

The RBI has issued Concentration Risk Management Directions for Local Area Banks effective immediately, establishing prudential exposure limits to mitigate risks from concentrated exposures to single counterparties or connected counterparty groups on both asset and liability sides of their balance sheets. Capital Funds for exposure norms comprise Tier I and Tier II capital as per the previous year's published accounts (with provisions for post-balance sheet capital infusions), while Exposure encompasses funded/non-funded credit limits, investments in shares/debentures/bonds/CPs, and derivative product exposures, with sanctioned limits or outstandings (whichever is higher) used for calculation purposes. These proportionately applicable limits strengthen LABs' overall risk management framework by restricting their concentration risk in line with broader RBI prudential norms established since 1989.

# RBI Master Directions Summary - Local Area Banks (Responsible Business Conduct) 2025

These Directions consolidate RBI's regulatory instructions on customer service and conduct for Local Area Banks, establishing a comprehensive framework for responsible banking practices covering institutional structures, customer protection, financial inclusion, lending conduct, and deposit management. LABs must comply with provisions on customer guidance, fair treatment, payment services, responsible lending practices, and standardized documentation procedures (outlined in multiple annexes) to ensure fair conduct and protect customer interests. The Directions come into effect immediately and apply to all Local Area Banks, with detailed definitions, institutional requirements, and operational standards designed to enhance service quality, ensure transparency, and safeguard customer rights across all banking operations.

The RBI has issued updated 'On tap' licensing guidelines for Small Finance Banks (SFBs) in the private sector, establishing a continuous application process to encourage competition beyond the initial ten licensed SFBs from 2014-2019. Eligible promoters must meet stringent capital requirements, corporate governance standards, and business plan criteria, with detailed provisions on promoter contribution, foreign shareholding limits, and voting rights to ensure effective control and financial stability. The guidelines also introduce a voluntary transition scheme for Urban Co-operative Banks to convert into SFBs, subject to specified financial benchmarks and procedural requirements including comprehensive documentation and RBI approval.

Banks with currency chests must report all transactions through ICCOMS on the same day by 9 PM, with link offices consolidating and reporting to Issue Offices by 11 PM; failure to meet these deadlines incurs penal interest calculated on a T+0 basis. Penal interest is levied for delayed, wrong, or non-reported currency chest transactions, with specific penalties including ₹50,000 flat fee for soiled note remittances incorrectly reported as withdrawals and ₹50,000 for delayed reporting of net deposit transactions to ensure reporting discipline. The Master Direction applies to all banks operating currency chests and State Treasuries, enforcing compliance with the RBI's Clean Note Policy through financial penalties and strict timelines for accurate transaction reporting.

# RBI Regulatory Summary

These Directions empower Rural Co-operative Banks (State and Central Co-operative Banks) to undertake diversified financial services including insurance business as corporate agents, merchant acquisition services, and issuance of pre-paid payment instruments, effective immediately from November 28, 2025. The Directions establish governance requirements for RCBs' Board oversight and regulate their investments in Alternative Investment Funds while defining the scope of permissible financial services businesses. RCBs must comply with these mandatory requirements to expand their service offerings while maintaining regulatory oversight through RBI's supervisory framework.

The RBI Directions, 2025 establish regulatory framework for All-India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID) to undertake financial services through subsidiaries and foreign operations with immediate effect. The Directions define key terms including financial services companies, capital funds, control, debtor companies, and equity instruments, while establishing prudential regulations for investments and procedures for applications under the Banking Regulation Act and RBI Act. AIFIs must comply with capital adequacy norms, investment restrictions, and governance requirements when establishing subsidiaries, branches, and operations in foreign jurisdictions and International Financial Services Centers (IFSCs).

These Directions, effective November 28, 2025, establish comprehensive regulatory requirements for All India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID) regarding classification, valuation, and operation of their investment portfolios across three categories: Held to Maturity (HTM), Available for Sale (AFS), and Held for Trading (HFT). The framework mandates board oversight of investment policies, prescribes specific valuation methodologies for different security types, and establishes prudential controls including internal governance, broker engagement rules, and strict audit and reporting requirements. Key provisions include requirements for current credit ratings on non-government securities, detailed settlement procedures for government and corporate securities, and accounting standards for income recognition, broken period interest, and non-performing investments through an Investment Reserve Account.

# RBI Directions Summary: Urban Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets (2025)

These Directions establish a consolidated framework for Urban Co-operative Banks to manage and resolve stressed assets through restructuring, compromise settlements, and technical write-offs, with harmonized prudential norms for asset classification, provisioning, and income recognition. The framework addresses special cases including fraud-affected accounts, natural calamity impacts, infrastructure projects, and Government Debt Relief Schemes, requiring UCBs to maintain board-approved policies for early identification and reporting of stressed assets. The Directions also lay out principles for UCB participation in State Government Debt Relief Schemes to mitigate credit discipline risks and moral hazard concerns while balancing fiscal support mechanisms with financial prudence.

The RBI has issued Master Directions for NBFCs on managing risks in outsourcing of financial and IT services, effective immediately, requiring compliance with governance frameworks including Board-approved policies, risk assessments, service provider evaluation, and robust oversight mechanisms. Existing IT outsourcing agreements must comply by April 10, 2026 (or at renewal, whichever is earlier), while new agreements must comply from their inception, covering activities that cannot be outsourced, confidentiality requirements, business continuity planning, and grievance redressal procedures. The directions apply to eleven categories of NBFCs on a layered basis, with Base layer NBFCs subject to non-IT chapters, while Middle and Upper layer NBFCs must comply with comprehensive IT outsourcing provisions including offshore/cross-border arrangements, cloud computing, and security operations center outsourcing.

# RBI Agency Banking Directions, 2026 - Summary

The RBI has issued directions governing how Agency Banks (public sector banks, scheduled private sector banks, payments banks, and small finance banks) conduct government business and claim agency commission for services rendered to Central and State Governments. The directions specify eligible government transactions for agency commission, establish commission rates, define reporting requirements through scrolls and luggage files, and outline procedures for claiming and reconciling payments with penalties for incorrect claims. Agency Banks are subject to RBI oversight for government business conducted, with clear definitions of prefunded schemes and transaction documentation requirements to ensure transparent and accountable conduct of government banking operations.

The RBI amended urban co-operative banks' (UCBs) credit facility directions effective October 1, 2026, restricting housing loan tenors to 20 years maximum for Tier 1-2 UCBs while allowing Tier 3-4 banks greater flexibility, and limiting moratorium periods to 24 months for under-construction houses only. The circular prohibited credit facilities against fixed deposits of other banks and revised unsecured advance limits to single borrowers based on UCB tier (₹5-10 lakh), while enhancing risk management requirements for housing loan pricing and portfolio management. These amendments aim to strengthen prudential norms and ensure UCBs maintain appropriate risk management frameworks aligned with borrower life expectancy and exposure duration.

Small Finance Banks must meet strict prudential requirements including maintaining regulatory capital compliance and positive adjusted Profit After Tax (adjusted for 50% of Net NPAs) to declare dividends starting FY 2026-27. Dividend payout is restricted based on Tier 1 Capital Ratio, ranging from 0% (below 7.5%) to 100% (above 19.5%) of adjusted PAT, with an aggregate cap of 75% of PAT. Boards must consider NPA divergence trends, audit findings, capital adequacy projections, and long-term growth plans, with exceptional/extraordinary profits excluded from dividend calculations and violations subject to penal consequences.

The RBI has amended income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning directions for Local Area Banks to align with new stressed asset resolution provisions effective July 1, 2026. Key amendments include: accounts under resolution plans may retain or be upgraded to 'Standard' classification, and repeatedly restructured accounts continue as 'Standard'; banks must maintain additional specific provisions of 5% of outstanding debt per restructuring instance (capped at 100%), reversible upon 20% debt repayment or after one year for non-fund-based facilities; and interest income recognition switches to accrual basis for resolution plan accounts and cash basis for repeatedly restructured accounts. This document is a Money Market Operations press release, not a regulatory circular. However, here are the key points:

The RBI's money market operations on May 22, 2026 showed overnight segment transactions of ₹7,24,966.79 crore at a weighted average rate of 5.26%, with Triparty Repo dominating activity. The RBI conducted liquidity absorption operations through repo and Standing Deposit Facility, resulting in net liquidity withdrawal of ₹54,977.42 crore to manage system liquidity. Scheduled commercial banks maintained cash balances of ₹7,91,444.90 crore against an average daily requirement of ₹7,96,910 crore, indicating a tight liquidity position with durable liquidity surplus of ₹3,03,862 crore as of April 30, 2026.

# Summary

Rural Co-operative Banks (State Co-operative Banks and District Central Co-operative Banks) must maintain Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) as prescribed by these RBI Directions, effective immediately, with CRR and SLR maintenance to be reported through specified statutory returns (Form B for scheduled banks, Form I for non-scheduled banks). SLR-compliant securities include dated Government of India securities, Treasury Bills, and State Development Loans, with only unencumbered portions qualifying as specified SLR assets, except for securities lodged as collateral that have not been drawn against. Banks must apportion Savings Bank Account deposits into demand and time liabilities using a half-yearly methodology based on minimum balance averages, with these proportions applied to all reporting fortnights in the subsequent six months.

Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) are now authorized to undertake specified financial services including mutual fund distribution, insurance business as corporate/referral agents, foreign exchange business, online trading facilities, pension fund services, merchant acquisition, PAN agent services, and pre-paid payment instruments—all subject to RBI's regulatory framework and board oversight. The directions emphasize that UCBs' boards bear responsibility for ensuring compliance with investments in Alternative Investment Funds and other prescribed activities while managing associated risks. These directions apply immediately to all primary co-operative banks operating in India and supersede previous regulations, requiring UCBs to align their financial service operations with RBI's defined parameters for public interest protection.

# RBI Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities Directions 2025 Summary

These Directions consolidate RBI's regulatory framework for credit facilities extended by State and Central Co-operative Banks, covering digital lending, gold/silver collateral loans, microfinance, housing loans, and non-fund-based facilities while establishing prudential safeguards and customer protection norms. Key requirements include mandatory board-approved credit policies, technology standards for digital lending through third-party service providers (LSPs), restrictions on loan-to-value ratios, household income assessment for microfinance, and specific eligibility criteria for housing loans. The framework aims to balance financial innovation and orderly credit growth with protection of depositors and borrowers' interests across rural credit delivery mechanisms.

The RBI amendment circular (RBI/2026-27/74) dated April 29, 2026 amends the Responsible Business Conduct Directions for All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) by adding Section 33A, which permits AIFIs to provide discretionary relief measures including fee and charge waivers or reductions for customers in calamity-declared areas for up to one year. The amendment becomes effective from July 1, 2026, and is issued under sections 45L of the RBI Act, 1934 to support responsible business conduct during natural disasters. This provision enables AIFIs to exercise flexibility in offering customer relief during declared calamities while maintaining their discretionary authority on the scope and nature of relief measures.

The RBI has amended the Commercial Banks – Credit Risk Management Directions by inserting Paragraph 12A, which requires banks to incorporate the potential impact of calamities on borrowers into their credit assessment processes. This amendment is issued under sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and is consequent to the Second Amendment Directions on Resolution of Stressed Assets from April 29, 2026. The new requirement becomes effective on July 1, 2026, and mandates enhanced due diligence in credit risk evaluation to account for borrowers' vulnerability to natural disasters and other calamitous events.

These Amendment Directions modernize rural cooperative banks' resolution framework for stressed assets by introducing standardized definitions for "date of invocation" and "natural calamity" (aligned with NDRF/SDRF recognition) and deleting outdated special restructuring provisions. Banks must now incorporate board-approved policies with objective principles, relief measures, and delegation matrices for timely implementation of calamity-related resolutions, while guidance follows Small Finance Banks' Resolution Directions, 2025 principles. The framework establishes SLBC/UTLBC/DCC coordination mechanisms to assess calamity impact within 15 days of declaration and formulate objective criteria for identifying affected borrowers and determining moratorium periods.

The RBI amended the Urban Cooperative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025 to align the definition of "financial difficulty" with that specified in the Small Finance Banks directions for consistency across regulatory frameworks. The amendment modifies the Explanation to paragraph 5(4)(v) to reference the standardized definition of financial difficulty, ensuring uniform interpretation across different bank categories. The amendment becomes effective from April 1, 2027, providing urban cooperative banks adequate time for implementation and compliance.

This Master Direction, updated as of February 16, 2026, consolidates RBI's regulatory framework for External Commercial Borrowings (ECB), Trade Credits (TC), and Structured Obligations under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, superseding earlier directions from January 1, 2016. The framework is implemented through FEMA Regulations on Borrowing and Lending (2018) and Guarantees (2026), with RBI issuing additional directions to Authorised Dealer banks to regulate how foreign exchange transactions are conducted. Authorised Persons must comply with these directions regarding ECB and TC transactions, with reporting requirements specified in the Master Direction on Reporting, and RBI reserves the right to issue further A.P. (DIR Series) Circulars to amend procedures or respond to regulatory changes.

# Summary of RBI Directions on NBFC Credit Card Issuance and Conduct (2025)

These Directions, effective immediately, establish comprehensive regulatory framework for NBFCs (NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-MFI, and HFC) to issue and conduct credit card business, covering conduct regulations, form factors, and co-branding arrangements while aligning with prudential and cybersecurity requirements. Key applicability covers definitions and conduct parameters for various credit card types including principal cards, add-on cards, co-branded cards, business credit cards, and charge cards, with standardized terms for billing cycles, credit limits, interest-free periods, and cardholder protections. NBFCs must comply with all prescribed terms and conditions for credit card issuance and operation, including restrictions on fees, loyalty programs, and convenience charges, to ensure consumer protection and regulated financial product delivery.

The RBI's Digital Payments E-mandate Framework, 2026 consolidates regulations for recurring transactions across cards, PPI, and UPI, requiring Payment System Providers to implement additional factor of authentication (AFA) for e-mandate registration and modifications, while allowing customers to specify validity periods, transaction amounts, and opt-out options. Key provisions establish transaction limits of ₹15,000 without AFA for standard recurring payments and ₹1,00,000 for insurance premiums/mutual funds/credit card payments, mandate pre-transaction notifications at least 24 hours before debits, and post-transaction notifications with grievance redressal details. The framework applies immediately to all domestic and cross-border recurring transactions, establishing robust dispute resolution mechanisms aligned with RBI's liability limits for unauthorized transactions.

# RBI Circular Summary

The RBI has eliminated the prior approval requirement for non-bank entities to facilitate outward remittances through Authorized Dealer (Category I) banks, replacing it with a streamlined framework where ADs must directly comply with specified operational guidelines. Authorized Dealers remain solely responsible for FEMA compliance, KYC verification, and all acts of third-party entities, and must prominently display FX rates, transaction costs, beneficiary credit amounts, and customer grievance contact details on all platforms. ADs must generate invoices with detailed cost breakdowns, maintain agreements ensuring third parties cannot dilute their regulatory obligations, and update their websites with all third-party arrangement details and customer data storage policies.

The RBI's 2025 Guidelines mandate that new foreign banks entering India must operate through Wholly Owned Subsidiaries (WOS) if they meet specified criteria (paragraph 3), while those not meeting these criteria may choose between WOS or branch mode, with mandatory conversion to WOS if criteria are later satisfied. Existing foreign banks that commenced operations before August 2010 retain the option to continue in branch mode or voluntarily convert to WOS, while those starting from August 2010 onwards must convert to WOS if required by the RBI. This framework aims to enhance financial stability, protect depositors, improve regulatory oversight, and facilitate resolution of foreign banks by creating separate legal entities with independent capital bases and local governance structures.

The RBI has amended the Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFC) Credit Risk Management Directions by inserting Paragraph 8A, requiring NBFCs to incorporate the potential impact of calamities on borrowers into their credit assessments. This amendment applies to all NBFCs regulated under the RBI, National Housing Bank Act, and Factoring Regulation Act, and comes into effect from July 1, 2026. The directive aims to enhance credit risk evaluation by ensuring NBFCs account for external shocks and catastrophic events when assessing borrower creditworthiness and loan repayment capacity.

The RBI has repealed the Master Direction on Relief Measures by Banks in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities (2018) effective July 1, 2026, replacing it with updated directions covering stressed asset resolution, income recognition, asset classification, provisioning, responsible business conduct, and credit risk management. Actions taken under the repealed directions remain valid and governed by their original provisions, with all prior approvals continuing in effect. The repeal does not affect any existing rights, obligations, liabilities, penalties, or ongoing investigations under the previous framework, which may continue to be enforced as if the old directions remained in force.

These Directions establish prudential norms for Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) to declare dividends, requiring compliance with capital adequacy ratios, Net Non-Performing Asset ratios below 5%, maintenance of CRR/SLR, and adequate provisions for NPAs and investments. UCBs with NNPA ratios between 5-10% may seek RBI Regional Office permission to declare dividends, while those exceeding 10% are prohibited from dividend distribution. The Directions, effective immediately from November 28, 2025, repeal all previous dividend-related guidance and require boards to consider capital adequacy and profitability outlook when declaring dividends on equity shares.

The RBI's Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025 establish comprehensive prudential guidelines for managing credit risk in State and Central Co-operative Banks through board-approved policies, statutory restrictions, regulatory restrictions, and property valuation requirements. The directions, effective immediately from November 28, 2025, apply mandatory frameworks for credit facilities including cash credit, current accounts, and overdraft arrangements, with specific provisions for security interest filing in CERSAI and empanelment of valuers. Rural co-operative banks must implement these directions to strengthen credit risk management practices and ensure prudential compliance across their lending operations and related party transactions.

The Money Transfer Service Scheme (MTSS) enables authorized Indian agents to disburse inward personal remittances from abroad to beneficiaries in India through partnerships with overseas money transfer companies, with only family maintenance and foreign tourist remittances permitted. Eligible applicants include Authorised Dealers Category-I banks, Category-II entities, FFMCs, Scheduled Commercial Banks, or the Department of Posts, with a minimum Net Owned Fund requirement of Rs. 50 lakh. The RBI regulates and authorizes Indian agents under Section 10(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, with applications submitted through APConnect or regional Foreign Exchange Department offices, and the scheme permits sub-agent appointments to expand the network while prohibiting outward remittances.

# RBI Amendment Directions Summary

The RBI has amended income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning norms for rural cooperative banks implementing resolution plans for stressed assets, effective July 1, 2026. Banks must maintain a 5% additional specific provision on outstanding debt for accounts under resolution plans, with write-back permitted once borrowers repay 20% of debt without slipping into NPA or requiring further restructuring. Accounts classified as NPA between calamity occurrence and resolution plan implementation shall be upgraded to 'Standard' status upon implementation, with subsequent classification governed by standard criteria.

NBFCs must upgrade NPA accounts to 'Standard' classification upon implementing resolution plans under Chapter VI-A of the Stressed Assets Directions, with accounts undergoing repeated restructuring continuing as 'Standard'. NBFCs are required to maintain an additional 5% specific provision on outstanding debt for resolution plan implementations and each subsequent restructuring instance, capped at 100%, which can be written back once borrowers pay 20% of outstanding debt without slipping into NPA. Interest income recognition shall be on an accrual basis for first-time resolution plan implementations but on a cash basis for repeatedly restructured accounts, with all amendments effective from July 1, 2026.

The RBI has amended the Regional Rural Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2026 to add provisions for banking services during declared calamities, effective July 1, 2026. Regional Rural Banks may operate from temporary premises for up to 30 days (with RBI approval for extensions) and must establish satellite offices, extension counters, or mobile banking facilities to serve affected areas, while immediately restoring ATM services with alternative cash arrangements. The amendment also permits banks to open small accounts for calamity-displaced persons without standard identification requirements and allows discretionary fee/charge waivers or reductions for affected customers for up to one year.

This RBI notification lists circulars that have been withdrawn as per the Regulatory Reform Agenda (RRA) 2.0 recommendations, spanning from 2015 to 2019 across multiple departments including Payment and Settlement Systems, Currency Management, and Financial Inclusion. The withdrawn circulars covered critical areas such as prepaid payment instruments (PPIs), Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) operations, customer protection in electronic payments, anti-money laundering standards, and relief measures for natural calamities. The withdrawal of these circulars indicates RBI's ongoing regulatory rationalization efforts to consolidate, streamline, or supersede outdated guidance with updated master directions and regulations.

The RBI Directions 2025 establish governance and operational requirements for five All-India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID), effective immediately. Key requirements include: boards must adopt policies on staff certifications for specialized operations and option premium deferrals; AIFIs must establish Audit Committees meeting at least six times annually to oversee audit functions and RBI compliance; and AIFIs may defer option premiums on derivatives only after conducting due diligence on user payment capacity and ensuring uniform premium recovery within the contract maturity period. These directions strengthen institutional governance, risk management, and regulatory compliance across major development finance institutions.

# RBI Master Direction on Market-makers in OTC Derivatives (2021)

This Master Direction, effective January 3, 2022, establishes regulatory framework for entities authorized to act as market-makers in OTC derivatives including foreign exchange forwards/options/swaps, currency swaps, bond forwards, and credit default swaps. The directions apply to eligible market participants and are issued under Sections 45W and 45U of the RBI Act, 1934, with reference to the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999. The framework aims to ensure standardized operations and risk management practices for OTC derivative market-making activities in India's financial markets.

The RBI Directions, 2025 require prior written approval from the Reserve Bank for any acquisition of control or 26% or more shareholding in regulated NBFCs (including NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, HFCs, and others), with limited exceptions for court-approved buybacks and capital reductions. These Directions apply to most categories of NBFCs but exclude Mortgage Guarantee Companies and NOFHCs, and become effective immediately from the date of issue. The regulations establish a comprehensive framework governing who can acquire significant stakes in NBFCs, strengthening RBI's oversight of ownership changes to protect depositors and financial system stability.

These RBI Directions establish a comprehensive regulatory framework for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) governing credit risk transfer and distribution mechanisms, including loan transfers, inter-bank participations, and borrower account transfers. RRBs are permitted only as transferors of stressed loans under specific conditions and cannot participate in other types of loan transfers as either transferors or transferees, with mandatory legal ownership transfer required to the extent of economic interest transferred. The framework aims to facilitate liquidity management, risk diversification, and market development while ensuring that all loan transfers comply with defined conditions on credit enhancement, default definitions, and economic interest allocation.

The RBI's Know Your Customer (KYC) Directions 2025 establish comprehensive anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing requirements for commercial banks, mandating customer identification procedures, due diligence measures, beneficial owner identification, and ongoing transaction monitoring aligned with FATF standards. The directions apply to all commercial banks and their foreign branches/subsidiaries, requiring adoption of the more stringent KYC/AML standards between RBI and host country regulations to prevent misuse of financial channels for illicit activities. Banks must implement robust governance frameworks, risk-based customer acceptance policies, enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers, simplified procedures for low-risk accounts, and reporting obligations to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India as per the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and related rules.

These Directions establish a comprehensive regulatory framework for Local Area Banks' deposit interest rate policies, covering domestic rupee deposits, non-resident rupee deposits, and foreign currency deposits with specific rules for current accounts, savings deposits, and term deposits. The framework prohibits certain practices (such as marking liens on non-resident deposits) while permitting flexibility in floating rate structures and additional interest provisions, with penalties specified for premature withdrawals. The Directions came into effect upon placement on RBI's website on November 28, 2025, and apply exclusively to Local Area Banks as defined under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

# RBI Local Area Banks Directions 2025 Summary

The RBI has issued Master Directions effective November 28, 2025, establishing comprehensive regulations for acquisition and holding of shares or voting rights in Local Area Banks to ensure diversified ownership and maintain "fit and proper" major shareholders on a continuing basis. The directions require prior RBI approval for acquisitions and mandate continuous monitoring arrangements including due diligence, detection of violations under Section 12B(1) of the Banking Regulation Act 1949, and regular reporting requirements. Aggregate holdings are defined broadly to include direct and indirect acquisitions through relatives, associate enterprises, group entities, promoters, mutual funds, collective investment schemes, venture capital funds, and alternative investment funds to prevent concentration of control.

ai_summary: The RBI has issued comprehensive governance directions for Non-Banking Financial Companies effective immediately, establishing a tiered regulatory framework with differentiated requirements for Base Layer (NBFCs-BL), Middle Layer (NBFCs-ML), and Upper Layer (NBFCs-UL) entities. The directions mandate board-level governance policies, risk management committees, compliance structures, and specific requirements for appointment of key managerial personnel, with provisions tailored to entity size and systemic importance. All NBFCs must comply with chapters applicable to their classification, except government-owned NBFCs which are exempt from compensation-related provisions, and NOFHCs which are excluded entirely from these governance directions.

# RBI NBFC Branch Authorisation Directions 2025 Summary

NBFCs are generally permitted to open branches in India without prior RBI approval, except deposit-taking NBFCs which face restrictions based on Net Owned Funds (NOF) and credit ratings: those with NOF ≤₹50 crore or below AA rating may only operate within their registered state, while those with NOF >₹50 crore and AA or above rating can operate anywhere in India. The Directions apply to specific NBFC categories (NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-MFI, HFCs, etc.) but exclude certain entities like NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, and MGCs. As a general policy, NBFCs are prohibited from opening new branches abroad, though existing overseas branches established and intimated to RBI before the Directions may continue operations.

# RBI Circular Summary: Rural Co-operative Banks Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025

These Directions establish comprehensive regulations for Rural Co-operative Banks (State and Central Co-operative Banks) governing the classification, valuation, and operation of their investment portfolios, effective immediately upon issuance. The regulations mandate Board approval of investment policies, risk management systems for non-SLR investments, and define categorization of investments as either Permanent or Current with specific valuation methodologies for each category. Key requirements include compliance with prudential limits on non-SLR securities, proper accounting for investment income recognition, maintenance of Investment Fluctuation Reserve, and adherence to settlement procedures for government securities and corporate bonds through designated platforms.

# RBI Directions 2026 - Summary

The Reserve Bank of India has issued new Asset Classification, Provisioning, and Income Recognition Directions effective April 1, 2027, introducing an Expected Credit Loss (ECL)-based provisioning framework with a forward-looking staging approach while retaining existing NPA classification norms to strengthen banking sector resilience and transparency. These Directions apply to all commercial banks (excluding small finance banks, payment banks, and local area banks) and mandate adoption of the Effective Interest Rate (EIR) method for income recognition, along with comprehensive model risk management principles for ECL calculations. Banks must implement robust credit risk management practices, maintain detailed disclosures on ECL methodologies, and establish regulatory probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), and exposure at default (EAD) parameters, with transition arrangements allowing gradual compliance through March 31, 2027.

The RBI has amended the Small Finance Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions to add provisions addressing banking services in calamity-affected areas, effective July 1, 2026. Small Finance Banks may operate temporarily displaced branches with RBI approval, must restore ATM services promptly, and may open small accounts for calamity-displaced persons without full documentation per KYC norms. Banks are permitted to provide relief measures such as fee waivers and charge reductions for calamity-affected customers for up to one year.

The RBI Amendment Directions 2026 introduce new provisions for urban cooperative banks to ensure banking service continuity in calamity-affected areas, including operating from temporary premises (with RBI approval beyond 30 days), establishing satellite offices and mobile banking facilities, and prioritizing ATM service restoration. Banks may open small accounts for displaced persons without full documentation and may waive or reduce fees/charges for affected customers for up to one year in declared calamity zones. These amendments to Chapter V (Financial Inclusion and Accessibility) become effective from July 1, 2026, strengthening banks' institutional responsibility to serve communities during natural disasters.

The RBI's 2025 Securitisation Directions establish comprehensive regulatory requirements for NBFCs engaging in securitisation transactions, including mandatory origination standards, minimum retention requirements (MRR), and strict asset eligibility criteria to ensure prudent risk distribution. The Directions apply to specified NBFC categories (NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-IFC, IDF-NBFC, and HFCs) but exclude certain NBFC types including P2P platforms, mortgage guarantee companies, and base-layer NBFCs without public funds. The framework emphasizes transparency through Simple, Transparent and Comparable (STC) securitisations, mandates capital requirements and detailed disclosures for securitisation exposures, and establishes due diligence and stress-testing requirements for investor NBFCs to promote financial stability.

# RBI Master Directions - Resolution of Stressed Assets (2025)

These Directions establish a comprehensive framework for commercial banks to identify, report, and resolve stressed assets within defined timelines, emphasizing early recognition and structured resolution processes including inter-creditor agreements and resolution plans. The regulations introduce prudential norms for asset restructuring, additional provisioning requirements for delayed implementation, and special treatment for government debt relief schemes while addressing concerns about credit discipline and moral hazard. Banks must obtain board-approved policies for stress resolution, maintain proper disclosures, and comply with asset classification and income recognition standards, with exemptions provided in specific cases such as natural calamities and trade relief measures to facilitate timely resolution of non-performing assets.

The RBI has issued the Foreign Exchange Management (Authorised Persons) Regulations, 2026, to rationalize the authorization framework for Authorised Persons under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, improving foreign exchange service delivery and reducing compliance burden. All Authorised Persons must comply with these new regulations, which supersede multiple earlier A.P. (DIR Series) Circulars dating back to 2000 and amend instructions in the Master Directions for Money Changing Activities and Other Remittance Facilities. These directions are issued under Sections 10(4) and 11 of the FEMA, 1999, and are effective without prejudice to any other required legal permissions or approvals.

# RBI Asset Reconstruction Companies – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025

The RBI has issued new KYC directions applicable to all Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), establishing comprehensive AML/CFT compliance requirements aligned with FATF standards and India's Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002. The directions mandate ARCs to implement customer acceptance policies, conduct customer identification procedures (CIP), perform customer due diligence (CDD), maintain detailed records, and report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India. These requirements cover beneficial owner identification, risk management frameworks, transaction monitoring, and international compliance obligations to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing through the ARC sector.

# Summary of RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Governance) Directions, 2025

The Reserve Bank of India has issued mandatory governance directions applicable to State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks, effective immediately, establishing requirements for board composition, director eligibility, and CEO/MD appointments. Rural Co-operative Banks must ensure their boards include at least two directors with banking experience or professional qualifications in accountancy, banking, agriculture, legal, or auditing fields, while excluding individuals engaged in money lending, those with criminal convictions involving moral turpitude, and non-members. The directions establish the Board's responsibility for policy formulation and overall supervision, mandate RBI approval for CEO/MD appointments through the PRAVAAH portal, and require banks to implement comprehensive codes of conduct for directors and senior management while ensuring all regulatory circulars are reviewed by board members.

The RBI Directions 2025 require Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) to report information on large defaulters (loans ≥₹1 crore) and wilful defaulters (≥₹25 lakh) to credit information companies monthly, with specific formats for suit-filed and non-suit-filed accounts classified as doubtful or loss. ARCs must promptly notify credit bureaus when borrowers' outstanding amounts fall below thresholds, except in compromise settlement cases where names remain on the wilful defaulter list until full payment is made. These restrictions on further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters apply to all RBI-regulated entities to prevent continued lending to chronic defaulters and protect the financial system.
