The directions establish comprehensive frameworks for credit information reporting, data quality management, consumer grievance redressal, and customer compensation mechanisms while safeguarding data confidentiality and security. These directions apply immediately to all Small Finance Banks and mandate compliance with standardized reporting timelines, data correction procedures, and use of credit reports in credit appraisal, along with appointment of Internal Ombudsmen for customer grievance resolution.

This amendment modifies Small Finance Banks' norms for income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning to align with RBI's stressed asset resolution framework effective July 1, 2026. Banks must maintain 5% additional specific provisioning for resolution plan implementations and repeated restructurings, with write-back provisions triggered upon 20% debt repayment without further defaults or restructuring. Interest income recognition shifts to accrual basis for resolution plan accounts and cash basis for restructured accounts, while accounts under resolution plans may retain or upgrade to 'Standard' classification despite prior NPA slippage.

The RBI has discontinued the Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR) requirement for Local Area Banks effective May 18, 2026, reflecting updated prudential frameworks for market risk and investment management. LABs must transfer their existing IFR balance as of May 17, 2026, to Statutory Reserve, General Reserve, or Balance of Profit & Loss Account on a below-the-line basis. Related paragraphs 105-107 of the 2025 Directions have been deleted, simplifying the regulatory framework for investment portfolio operations.

The RBI's Rural Co-operative Banks Voluntary Amalgamation Directions, 2025, establish a regulatory framework for merging State Co-operative Banks (StCBs) and District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs) through a two-stage approval process requiring shareholder approval by two-thirds majority and RBI sanction following NABARD consultation. The directions cover two amalgamation scenarios: one or more DCCBs merging with a StCB, or one DCCB merging with another DCCB, with State Governments required to conduct detailed studies demonstrating financial viability, capital support strategy, and governance models before submission. The implementation process mandates public notice of shareholder meetings in local newspapers for three consecutive weeks and compliance with legal requirements, court orders, and regulatory criteria, ensuring transparent and structured consolidation of rural cooperative banking institutions.

# RBI Payments Banks Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025 Summary

These Master Directions establish prudential norms for capital adequacy applicable to all Payments Banks under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, effective immediately upon issuance in November 2025 (updated May 2026). The directions comprehensively define regulatory capital components (CET 1, AT 1, and Tier 2 capital), prescribe minimum capital requirements, and detail risk-weighted asset (RWA) calculations for credit risk, market discipline, and leverage ratio frameworks. Payments Banks must comply with all capital adequacy norms, leverage ratio requirements, and regulatory adjustments while ensuring permissibility of activities under extant statutory and regulatory frameworks, with specific reporting obligations for capital issuances and FII/NRI investments in AT1 instruments.

# RBI Payments Banks Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025 Summary

These Directions establish mandatory classification, valuation, and operational requirements for payments banks' investment portfolios, effective immediately, covering investments categorized as Held-to-Maturity (HTM), Available-for-Sale (AFS), and Fair-Value-Through-Profit-and-Loss (FVTPL) with specific measurement and recognition standards. Payments banks must implement robust board-level investment policy frameworks, conduct fair value assessments using quoted market prices or acceptable valuation models for unquoted securities, and maintain stringent internal controls and audit procedures for portfolio management and governance. The circular mandates detailed income recognition protocols, non-performing investment classifications, maintenance of investment fluctuation reserves, and strict operational guidelines for government and non-SLR securities, ensuring regulatory compliance and financial stability in payments banks' investment activities.

The Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025, establish a regulatory framework for voluntary mergers of urban co-operative banks, requiring two-third board majority approval from both entities and ensuring the amalgamating bank protects all depositors' deposits while maintaining minimum Capital Adequacy Ratio (CRAR) requirements post-merger. The directions mandate comprehensive due diligence, independent valuation of swap ratios, and strict adherence to RBI shareholding guidelines and cooperative society laws, with assets incorporated at existing carrying amounts without upward revaluation. RBI approval is contingent upon demonstrating that the merger strengthens the combined entity's financial position, including profitability, asset quality, and regulatory compliance, while protecting depositor interests irrespective of the amalgamated bank's net worth status.

# RBI Directions on Government Pension Disbursement by Agency Banks (2026)

These directions mandate that Agency Banks (PSBs, PVBs, Payments Banks, and SFBs) promptly implement all Government orders regarding pension disbursement, including Dearness Relief, by directly accessing Government websites without waiting for RBI forwarding, and credit pension amounts to pensioners' accounts based on orders from Pension Sanctioning Authorities. Agency Banks must refund excess pension payments to Government immediately if errors occur on their part, while establishing clear procedures for handling Government-caused errors, alongside ensuring customer service standards including timely pension credits, life certificates through Jeevan Pramaan, and compensation for payment delays. The directions also require banks to display pension withdrawal guidelines, appoint Nodal Officers for customer grievances, and maintain sympathetic treatment of pensioners consistent with the Prabhakar Rao Committee recommendations.

The RBI amendment directive of April 27, 2026 adds "AgriSURE - Agri Fund for Start Ups & Rural Enterprises" to Annex I of the Urban Co-operative Banks Directions, expanding the permitted financial services that urban co-operative banks may undertake. The amendment is issued under sections 35A and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, in the public interest to regulate urban co-operative bank operations. The directive became effective immediately upon issuance, enabling eligible urban co-operative banks to participate in agricultural and rural enterprise financing initiatives.

# RBI Local Area Banks Debit Card Directions 2025 - Summary

These Directions establish regulatory requirements for Local Area Banks issuing debit cards (including co-branded variants), mandating Board-approved policies covering issuance, co-branding arrangements, card blocking procedures, and grievance redressal frameworks. Debit cards may only be issued to customers with Savings Bank or Current Accounts, and cannot be forced upon customers or linked to other banking facilities, while banks must comply with existing RBI prudential, payment, and cybersecurity directives. The Directions take immediate effect and supersede previous regulations, establishing comprehensive conduct standards for debit card operations including form factors, loyalty programs, convenience fees, and consumer protection measures across all Local Area Banks.

# RBI Amendment Directions Summary: Regional Rural Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets (2026)

The amendment expands the scope of resolution guidelines for Regional Rural Banks to cover accounts impacted by natural calamities and external events (riots/disturbances) recognized by Central/State Governments, replacing the previous Part B with a new Chapter IV-A that aligns prudential norms across regulated entities. Banks must adopt board-approved policies incorporating objective relief principles, verifiable parameters, and delegation matrices for timely implementation of restructuring and relief measures for affected borrowers. State Level Bankers' Committees (SLBC)/District Consultative Committees (DCC) must convene meetings within 15 days of calamity declaration to assess impact, formulate objective criteria for identifying affected borrowers, and determine necessary resolution measures, while existing accounts receiving prior relief continue under previous guidelines unless fresh resolutions are required.

The RBI's Currency Distribution & Exchange Scheme (CDES) provides financial incentives to bank branches and currency chests for improving customer service in note and coin exchange, aligned with the Clean Note Policy objectives. Banks receive incentives including 50% reimbursement of capital costs (up to ₹50 lakh) for opening currency chests in underbanked areas with populations under 1 lakh, partial revenue cost recovery for 3-5 years, and per-unit payments for soiled note exchanges (₹2 per packet), mutilated note adjudication (₹2 per piece), and coin distribution (₹25 per bag). Incentives are automatically paid without separate claims when soiled notes and adjudicated notes are received at RBI Issue Offices, with currency chest branches distributing payments pro-rata to linked branches based on actual service delivery.

The RBI has issued a Master Direction establishing the Currency Distribution & Exchange Scheme (CDES) to incentivize banks in providing better currency exchange and distribution services while supporting the Clean Note Policy objectives. Banks receive financial incentives for operating currency chests in remote areas (up to 100% capital cost reimbursement and 50% revenue cost for 5 years), exchanging soiled notes (₹2 per packet), adjudicating mutilated notes (₹2 per piece), and distributing coins (₹65 per bag, plus ₹10 additional for rural areas). Service charges for non-chest branch deposits at currency chests increased to ₹11 per 100 pieces for large modern chests and ₹8 per 100 pieces for other chests, effective October 1, 2025, with incentives paid on actual receipts verified through RBI inspections and to be distributed pro-rata among linked branches.

# RBI Circular Summary: Local Area Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025

These Directions establish prudential norms for Local Area Banks regarding income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning for their advances portfolio, effective immediately, to ensure greater consistency and transparency in financial reporting aligned with international practices. The Directions define key classifications including Non-Performing Assets (income-ceasing assets), Doubtful Assets (substandard for 12+ months), Loss Assets, and Substandard Assets, with specific criteria for determining "out of order" status for cash credit/overdraft accounts based on 90-day periods of excess limits or insufficient credits. Banks must follow prescribed provisioning norms, maintain adequate coverage ratios, reverse income upon NPA classification, and appropriately utilize floating provisions while adhering to the Board's role in overseeing prudent lending practices and consumer education requirements.

These RBI Directions 2025 establish comprehensive credit risk management requirements for five All India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID), effective immediately upon issuance. Key requirements include board-approved credit policies, legal entity identifier (LEI) registration for borrowers, mandatory filing of security interests in CERSAI for immovable/movable/intangible assets, and regulatory restrictions on lending to related parties through a dedicated committee. The directions aim to strengthen prudential tools and systemic risk management across AIFIs' varied sectoral exposures through statutory restrictions and enhanced credit governance frameworks.

# RBI Master Direction - Call, Notice and Term Money Markets (2021)

The Reserve Bank has issued comprehensive directions regulating call money (overnight unsecured borrowing/lending), notice money (up to 14 days), and term money markets, effective April 5, 2021, superseding previous directions from 2016-2020. The directions establish eligibility criteria, trading mechanisms, and operational frameworks for banks, primary dealers, and other market participants, utilizing platforms like NDS-CALL and electronic trading platforms for transactions. Participants must comply with capital adequacy requirements, reporting obligations, and market conduct standards as defined in the directions, with the RBI maintaining regulatory oversight through specified documentation and audit requirements.

These directions establish comprehensive governance frameworks for public sector, private sector, and foreign commercial banks in India, effective immediately, covering board composition, director appointments, and key officer roles including Chief Risk Officer, Chief Financial Officer, and Chief Vigilance Officer. The directions apply to all commercial banks (excluding Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks) and are subject to existing statutory provisions, with non-scheduled banks exempted from certain Chief Risk Officer and Chief Financial Officer requirements. RRBs must comply with these Directions alongside existing RBI directives on prudential matters, payment systems, and cybersecurity while ensuring transparent disclosure of Annual Percentage Rates, billing cycles, and convenience fees to cardholders.

# RBI Regulatory Document Summary

The RBI has issued new Master Directions for All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) including EXIM Bank, NABARD, NaBFID, NHB, and SIDBI, establishing resource-raising norms with an Umbrella Limit (UL) capped at 100% of Net Owned Funds through four specified instruments: term deposits, term money borrowings, certificates of deposit, and commercial papers. # Summary of RBI Master Direction on Electronic Trading Platforms, 2025

These Directions supersede the 2018 framework and apply to all entities operating Electronic Trading Platforms (ETPs) for transactions in eligible instruments including securities, money market instruments, forex, and derivatives, effective immediately. Scheduled commercial banks and standalone primary dealers operating electronic systems where they are the sole price provider are exempt from these Directions, though they must comply with reporting requirements and can be mandated to follow the Directions if RBI deems it necessary for public interest. The revised framework introduces updated definitions and regulatory requirements for ETP operators, including provisions for algorithmic trading and key managerial personnel oversight, replacing the previous October 2018 directions based on feedback from stakeholders.

This Sixth Amendment Directions circular modifies the Reserve Bank of India's Commercial Banks Financial Statements Directions 2025, clarifying definitions of "Revenue Reserve" to exclude amounts retained for depreciation, asset diminution, or known liabilities, and updating presentation requirements for such reserves in Schedule 2(IV). The amendment introduces standardized disclosure requirements for "Movement of Provisions for Non-Performing Investments (NPIs)" with a four-line table format showing opening balance, provisions made, write-offs/write-backs, and closing balance in rupees crore for comparative reporting. These changes, effective immediately from May 18, 2026, align financial statement presentation with the Investment Portfolio Classification Directions and enhance transparency in banks' provision management and reserve reporting.

The Master Direction establishes RBI's framework for compounding FEMA 1999 contraventions under Section 15, empowering the Reserve Bank to settle violations (except Section 3(a)) through an application-based process completed within 180 days. Compounding authority is delegated based on contravention amounts: Assistant General Manager for up to Rs. 10 lakhs, Deputy General Manager for Rs. 10-40 lakhs, and General Manager for Rs. 40 lakhs and above, with penalties calculated up to three times the contravened amount or Rs. 2 lakhs for non-quantifiable breaches. All Authorised Dealer Category-I banks and Authorised banks must inform constituents of this compounding process and comply with reporting requirements, thereby providing a structured mechanism for voluntary settlement while discouraging willful violations.

This Master Direction consolidates RBI's IT governance requirements, effective April 1, 2024, applicable to commercial banks, select NBFCs, payments banks, small finance banks, credit information companies, and major financial institutions. The directive mandates comprehensive IT governance frameworks including board oversight through dedicated IT committees, robust infrastructure management, cybersecurity policies, vulnerability assessments, business continuity plans, and information systems audits. Regulated entities must establish IT steering committees, implement cryptographic controls, conduct regular penetration testing, maintain audit trails, and ensure disaster recovery capabilities to strengthen operational resilience and information security across the financial sector.

# RBI Payments Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares Directions 2025

These Directions establish regulatory requirements for major shareholders of Payments Banks to maintain "fit and proper" status on a continuous basis, requiring prior RBI approval for acquisition of shares or voting rights and comprehensive due diligence procedures. The Directions define "acquisition" broadly to include direct and indirect shareholding through relatives, associate enterprises, and related entities, with detailed provisions for calculating aggregate holdings across multiple ownership structures. Payments Banks must implement continuous monitoring arrangements, report violations of shareholding limits, and comply with prescribed lock-in periods and voting rights ceilings, with the framework applicable immediately upon publication on the RBI website.

# Summary of RBI Regional Rural Banks Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025

These Directions establish a standardized framework for Regional Rural Banks to report credit information to Credit Information Companies (CICs), requiring all RRBs to become members of all four RBI-registered CICs with capped membership fees (₹10,000 one-time, ₹5,000 annual per CIC). Credit institutions must report using standardized non-proprietary formats (Uniform Credit Reporting Format) across consumer, commercial, and microfinance segments, with prescribed timelines and data quality standards. The framework includes safeguards for data confidentiality, customer access to credit information, grievance redressal mechanisms, and compensation frameworks to protect consumer interests and ensure transparent credit appraisal practices.

# RBI Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk Directions, 2025

Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are now regulated under a comprehensive framework for credit risk transfer and distribution, with UCBs permitted only as transferors of stressed loans while being restricted from other types of loan transfers or acquisitions. The directions mandate that legal ownership of loans must be transferred to the extent of economic interest transferred, and all loan transfers must comply with specific provisions governing consortium arrangements, credit enhancement, and risk distribution mechanisms. These regulations come into effect immediately upon placement on the RBI website and apply exclusively to Primary Co-operative Banks as defined under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, establishing stricter controls compared to commercial banks.

The RBI Master Direction establishes a comprehensive framework combining incentive schemes to encourage banks to set up Currency Chest infrastructure and facilitate note/coin distribution, alongside penalty provisions for deficiencies in customer service and inaccurate reporting of currency transactions. The directive applies to all banks, with specific penal provisions for Currency Chest operations, and consolidates all previous guidelines on the subject into a single Master Direction effective from its publication date. Banks must ensure timely and accurate reporting of Currency Chest transactions while providing proper customer service through branches and ATMs, with penalties including penal interest for non-compliance.

The RBI's Credit Information Companies (Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025, establish comprehensive governance and risk management requirements for CICs outsourcing material IT services, including infrastructure, cloud computing, security solutions, and data center operations. CICs must implement board-approved outsourcing policies, conduct rigorous service provider evaluations, establish robust monitoring frameworks, and maintain confidentiality and security protocols, with existing agreements requiring compliance by April 10, 2026, and new agreements compliant immediately. The Directions exclude certain services from applicability, such as corporate internet banking from regulated entities, external audit services, and IT hardware/software procurement, while mandating specific provisions for group outsourcing, offshore arrangements, cloud services, and security operations centers to mitigate operational and security risks.

# RBI Master Direction – Facility for Exchange of Notes and Coins Summary

All bank branches across India are mandated to provide free exchange facilities for soiled, mutilated, and imperfect notes and coins to both customers and non-customers without discrimination on all working days, with coins in denominations of 50 paise to ₹20 remaining legal tender. Banks must actively publicize these facilities, refuse no small denomination notes or coins at counters, and keep sachets of coins at counters for customer convenience, while Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks may optionally exchange mutilated notes. The directive delegates powers to bank branches under the RBI (Note Refund) Rules, 2009 (as amended) to process refunds for mutilated/imperfect notes as a matter of grace, with monitoring requirements and mandatory staff training to ensure consistent implementation across all branches.

# RBI Local Area Banks Interest Rates Directions 2025 Summary

Local Area Banks must adopt a Board-approved comprehensive interest rate policy for all advances including microfinance loans, with floating rate loans priced against specified benchmarks (RBI Repo Rate, Government Treasury Bills, or other FBIL-published rates) by adding a bank-determined spread. Banks have flexibility to offer fixed or floating rate advances, must charge interest monthly (except agricultural advances which may use annual rests), and fixed rate loans below three years cannot be less than the benchmark rate for similar tenor.

# Summary of RBI Small Finance Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025

The directions establish comprehensive frameworks for Small Finance Banks to manage liquidity and interest rate risks through board oversight, liquidity policies, and detailed governance structures. Key requirements include implementing Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) standards, managing intraday liquidity, stress testing, and maintaining contingency funding plans with specific asset classifications and cash flow calculations. Banks must report regulatory returns on liquidity risk and interest rate risk monitoring, with compliance enforced through internal controls, management information systems, and periodic disclosures to ensure financial stability and depositor protection.

The RBI Master Directions for Small Finance Banks (2025) establish comprehensive governance and operational frameworks applicable to all small finance banks, including mandatory board-approved policies on donations, certifications, and mandatory leave requirements for sensitive positions. Key regulatory areas covered include the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund management, KYC updation procedures, prohibition on accepting deposits from private financiers, restrictions on derivative contracts and lottery ticket sales, and compliance with FATCA registration requirements. Banks must implement due diligence procedures for option premium deferment, maintain board oversight of director competencies in emerging technologies, and adhere to mandatory leave rotation policies for staff in sensitive positions while furnishing regular information and returns to the RBI.

# RBI Master Direction Summary: Rupee/Foreign Currency Vostro Accounts for Non-resident Exchange Houses

Authorised Category I banks may open and maintain Rupee/Foreign Currency Vostro accounts for non-resident Exchange Houses from Gulf countries, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, and FATF-compliant nations to facilitate cross-border inward remittances through Rupee Drawing Arrangements (RDAs). Banks must conduct thorough due diligence on Exchange Houses' financial standing and verify valid licenses from local authorities, with comprehensive legal documentation required for all arrangements. Once RDAs reach twenty in number, banks must commission detailed external audits of their internal systems and obtain Board authorization before establishing additional arrangements, with notification to the Reserve Bank required for all new tie-ups.

The Reserve Bank of India's 2025 Directions establish mandatory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements for commercial banks, applicable with immediate effect to all scheduled banking companies excluding small finance banks, local area banks, and payments banks. Commercial banks must maintain specified reserves and report CRR maintenance through Form A and SLR maintenance through Form VIII, with SLR assets comprising unencumbered Government of India securities, Treasury Bills, and State Development Loans, though certain collateralized securities qualify as SLR-compliant assets. The framework includes penalties for non-compliance and detailed computation procedures for apportioning savings bank deposits between demand and time liabilities on a half-yearly basis for regulatory reporting purposes.

# Master Direction - Insurance Summary

RBI consolidated existing instructions on insurance under FEMA 1999, regulating foreign exchange transactions for general, health, and life insurance policies. Residents in India may hold health/general insurance from foreign insurers within Liberalised Remittance Scheme limits, but Indian marine hull insurance covering war risks must be obtained only from Indian insurers; life insurance from foreign insurers requires RBI permission. Maturity proceeds or claim amounts from foreign life insurance policies must be repatriated to India within seven days through normal banking channels, with all transactions conducted by Authorised Persons in accordance with amended regulations issued periodically through RBI circulars.

# Summary of RBI's Local Area Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters Directions, 2025

These Directions establish a transparent, non-discriminatory procedure for Local Area Banks to classify borrowers as wilful defaulters while ensuring principles of natural justice are observed, with the objective of disseminating credit information to prevent further institutional finance to such defaulters. The Directions define wilful defaulters, large defaulters, and related terms, and require banks to establish an Identification Committee comprising a Whole-Time Director and senior officials to classify defaulters based on specified criteria including fund diversion, asset concealment, and fraudulent conduct. The restrictions on financial accommodation to wilful defaulters apply across all RBI-regulated entities, with mandatory reporting to Credit Information Companies and implementation of preventive measures by bank auditors to ensure compliance with these regulatory requirements.

The RBI Amendment Directions, 2026 modifies the Non-Banking Financial Companies–Undertaking of Financial Services Directions, 2025 by adding "AgriSURE - Agri Fund for Start Ups & Rural Enterprises" to Annex I, expanding the scope of eligible financial service undertakings. The amendment is issued under powers conferred by the RBI Act, 1934, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, and the National Housing Bank Act, and comes into force with immediate effect from April 27, 2026. This expansion is intended to promote financial inclusion and support agricultural entrepreneurship through regulated non-banking financial services channels.

The RBI's Rural Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025 establish a comprehensive framework for early identification, reporting, and time-bound resolution of stressed assets in State and Central Co-operative Banks, effective immediately. The Directions standardize prudential norms for restructuring accounts, compromise settlements, and technical write-offs while addressing government debt relief schemes (DRS) to balance credit discipline with borrower support. Banks must maintain board-approved policies for stress management, implement timely disclosures, and follow stringent statutory requirements where applicable, with special provisions for natural calamities and trade relief measures to facilitate systematic asset resolution across the rural cooperative banking sector.

These directions apply to various NBFC categories (NBFC-D, ICC, Factor, MFI, IFC, IDF-NBFC) plus HFCs and certain mortgage guarantee companies, with specific exemptions for NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, CICs, and NBFCs without public funds or customer interface. The directions require NBFCs to implement exposure limits, manage counterparty concentration, track connected party relationships, and comply with category-specific regulatory restrictions that become progressively more stringent from base to upper layer NBFCs.

# RBI Relief Measures Directions 2018 - Summary

The RBI issued consolidated master directions requiring all scheduled commercial banks (including Small Finance Banks) to establish pre-approved board-level policies and procedures for providing rapid relief in natural calamity-affected areas, covering loan restructuring, fresh loans, and ancillary assistance. Banks must empower their Divisional/Zonal Managers with discretionary authority to expedite relief measures and ensure coordination with government authorities through standing instructions activated immediately upon official calamity declaration. The framework applies uniformly across all SCBs to enable swift, coordinated action addressing the economic rehabilitation needs of borrowers affected by twelve recognized types of natural calamities (cyclone, drought, earthquake, flood, tsunami, etc.) identified under the National Disaster Management Framework.

Banks must report all currency chest transactions through the CyM-CC portal by 7 pm on the same business day, with penal interest levied on delayed, wrong, or non-reported transactions calculated on a T+0 basis from the date of non-compliance. Penal interest is also imposed when ineligible amounts (such as cash not freely available to joint custodians or held in sealed covers) are incorrectly included in chest balances, calculated from inclusion until exclusion of such amounts. The penal interest rates and additional penalties for shortages, pilferage, fraud, or counterfeit notes are specified in the accompanying scheme of penalties to ensure discipline and accuracy in currency chest operations.

Banks are mandated to provide comprehensive currency exchange facilities at all branches nationwide, including issuing fresh notes/coins, exchanging soiled or mutilated notes, and accepting coins without discrimination on all working days, with select branches offering Sunday services. All bank branches have been delegated powers to exchange mutilated or defective notes free of cost under the RBI (Note Refund) Rules 2009, and banks must accept all legal tender coins and notes including small denominations without refusal. The definition of "soiled notes" has been liberalized to include two-piece notes pasted together with no missing features, facilitating faster exchanges, though these notes must be deposited in currency chests rather than re-issued to the public.

# RBI Amendment Directions Summary - Small Finance Banks Stressed Assets Resolution

The RBI has amended its directions on resolution of stressed assets in small finance banks to rationalize prudential norms for exposures affected by natural calamities (recognized under NDRF/SDRF) or external events like riots causing economic loss. Banks must now incorporate board-approved policies for calamity-linked resolution, including objective relief principles, relief measures with verifiable parameters, and delegation matrices for timely implementation. The new Chapter VI-A establishes a framework requiring State/District Level Bankers' Committees to convene meetings within 15 days of a calamity declaration to assess impact severity, formulate objective borrower identification criteria, and determine moratorium periods, with decisions communicated to RBI's Regional Offices.

# RBI Commercial Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025

The RBI has issued comprehensive Master Directions establishing mandatory Asset Liability Management (ALM) frameworks for commercial banks, covering liquidity risk management (including Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio requirements), intraday liquidity monitoring, and interest rate risk management. Banks must implement robust governance structures with board-level oversight, maintain high-quality liquid assets, diversify funding sources, and conduct regular stress testing and contingency planning to ensure financial stability. The directions require banks to comply with multiple regulatory reporting standards including contractual maturity analysis, funding concentration monitoring, and interest rate sensitivity assessments, with specific disclosure requirements and monitoring tools tailored to different bank categories.

# RBI Payments Banks Governance Directions, 2025 - Summary

These Directions establish comprehensive governance requirements for Payments Banks, including mandatory board composition, appointment procedures for directors and senior management (MD&CEO, Chief Risk Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Chief Technical Officer), with specific exemptions for non-scheduled Payment Banks from certain provisions. Banks must implement robust due diligence processes using "fit and proper" criteria for director appointments, establish a Nomination and Remuneration Committee for oversight, and comply with remuneration frameworks including malus and clawback provisions for material risk takers and control function staff. The Directions came into force immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025, and require strict regulatory compliance with periodic reporting to RBI.

These Master Directions establish comprehensive governance and risk management requirements for commercial banks outsourcing financial services and IT operations, with the Board responsible for approving outsourcing policies and ensuring accountability while prohibiting outsourcing of certain critical functions. Banks must implement robust frameworks covering service provider evaluation, security protocols, business continuity planning, and monitoring controls, with existing IT outsourcing agreements required to comply by April 10, 2026, while new agreements must comply immediately upon execution. The Directions apply to all Scheduled Commercial Banks and create a "comply or explain" approach for foreign bank branches, strengthening RBI's oversight of outsourced activities to mitigate operational, security, and financial risks.

Small Finance Banks must obtain RBI prior approval before launching transactional digital banking facilities and must submit a Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy (GAICA) report within 30 days of commencing view-only banking services, with eligibility requiring Core Banking Solution implementation and IPv6-enabled IT infrastructure. Banks must establish comprehensive policies for all digital banking channels addressing statutory and regulatory requirements, operational risk management, and liquidity management, distinguishing between view-only facilities (balance enquiries, statement downloads) and transactional facilities (fund transfers, loans). These Directions, effective January 1, 2026, apply to all Small Finance Banks operating in India and establish mandatory prudential guidelines and technological standards for digital banking channel authorization and operation.

These Directions establish comprehensive regulatory framework for All India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID) to conduct securitisation transactions with requirements covering asset eligibility, minimum retention of exposures, origination standards, and investor due diligence. The framework distinguishes between simple, transparent and comparable (STC) securitisations and other structures, with specific capital requirements, disclosure norms, and prudential oversight obligations for each category. AIFIs must implement stress testing, credit monitoring, and meet representations and warranties standards while maintaining bankruptcy-remote special purpose entities, with non-compliance carrying regulatory consequences under the RBI Act, 1934.

# Summary of RBI Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025

Urban Co-operative Banks must establish standardized credit information reporting to Credit Information Companies (CICs) using the non-proprietary Uniform Credit Reporting Format (UCRF), with membership mandatory in all four RBI-registered CICs at capped fees of ₹10,000 one-time and ₹5,000 annually per CIC. The directions establish frameworks for data accuracy, timely reporting and updation, customer access to credit information, grievance redressal mechanisms, and compensation provisions to protect consumer interests and ensure data confidentiality and security. These regulations apply immediately to all Urban Co-operative Banks and aim to create a standardized, transparent credit information ecosystem while safeguarding sensitive financial data and enabling customers to address discrepancies in their credit reports through established grievance mechanisms.

The RBI (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 establish comprehensive regulatory requirements for Local Area Banks covering governance, depositor protection, investment limits, compliance, and operational standards. Key provisions include mandatory Board-approved policies for alternative investment fund investments, donations, staff certifications, and mandatory leave for sensitive positions, along with strict compliance with FATCA registration and prohibitions on accepting deposits from private financiers and prize chit schemes. The directions implement controls on financial conduct, require depositor education fund contributions, and establish reporting requirements to ensure sound banking practices and consumer protection within the local banking sector.

RBI's Master Directions 2024 establish a comprehensive fraud risk management framework for all Urban, State, and Central Cooperative Banks, requiring them to implement Board-approved policies with robust governance structures and defined roles for fraud prevention and detection. All cooperative banks must adhere to principles of natural justice, including issuing Show Cause Notices (minimum 21 days response period) and serving reasoned orders before classifying accounts as fraudulent, with mandatory reporting to Law Enforcement Agencies and RBI within stipulated timeframes. The directions supersede previous 2015 guidelines and mandate early warning systems, staff accountability measures, legal audits for large-value loans, and specific protocols for cheque-related frauds and theft/robbery cases, strengthening the banking sector's fraud prevention infrastructure.

These 2026 RBI Directions establish the framework for Agency Banks (PSBs, scheduled PVBs, PBs, and SFBs) to conduct government banking business for Central and State Governments, with Agency Commission payable by RBI as remuneration for services excluding public debt management functions. The Directions detail eligible and ineligible government transactions for commission, reporting requirements through scrolls and luggage files, commission rates, and procedures for claiming commissions with supporting documentation. Banks face penal interest charges for incorrect commission claims, while RBI maintains oversight of government business conduct through compliance monitoring and regulatory oversight mechanisms.

# RBI Master Directions on Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs) - Summary

These Master Directions, issued under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 and updated through December 27, 2024, establish a comprehensive regulatory framework applicable to all banks and non-bank entities issuing PPIs, requiring RBI authorization for any entity setting up payment systems for PPIs. The framework aims to foster competition and innovation while ensuring system safety, customer protection, and interoperability, with specific eligibility criteria, net-worth requirements, and operational conditions for PPI issuers. Key provisions distinguish between Closed System PPIs (not RBI-regulated as they restrict purchases to the issuer only) and regulated open PPIs, and establish definitions for issuers, holders, merchants, and transaction limits denominated in INR.

# RBI Master Directions on Regional Rural Banks – Credit Facilities (2025)

These Directions consolidate RBI's regulatory framework for Regional Rural Banks' credit operations, covering digital lending, gold/silver collateral loans, microfinance, non-fund-based facilities, and housing loans with prudential norms and customer protection safeguards. The master directions establish mandatory board-approved policies, conduct requirements for bank-LSP arrangements, collateral valuation standards, loan-to-value ratios, household income assessments, and repayment obligation limits to ensure orderly growth and financial stability. RRBs must comply with these provisions immediately upon issuance, which supersede previous individual instructions and are enforceable under Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

All India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, NaBFID) must become members of all RBI-registered Credit Information Companies and report credit data using the standardized Uniform Credit Reporting Format (UCRF) with membership fees capped at ₹10,000 one-time and ₹5,000 annually per CIC. The directions establish a comprehensive framework for credit information reporting, dissemination, data security, consumer access, and grievance redressal mechanisms to ensure standardized, secure, and transparent credit information management across all India Financial Institutions. These directions come into force immediately and override previous instructions, requiring CIs to comply with specified data formats, reporting timelines, customer service standards, and compensation frameworks for affected customers.

The RBI has amended the Small Finance Banks Directions by adding "AgriSURE - Agri Fund for Start Ups & Rural Enterprises" to Annex I of the undertaking of financial services framework, effective immediately as of April 27, 2026. This amendment expands the scope of financial services that Small Finance Banks are authorized to undertake, specifically enabling them to participate in agricultural financing initiatives targeting startups and rural enterprises. The change is issued under section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and is deemed necessary in the public interest to support agricultural and rural economic development.

The RBI's Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025 establish comprehensive prudential requirements for managing credit risk across various NBFC categories (NBFC-D, NBFC-ICC, NBFC-Factor, NBFC-MFI, HFCs, etc.), with specific applicability layers and exclusions for certain entity types like NBFC-P2P and CICs. The directions mandate board-approved credit risk policies, standardized credit evaluation procedures, regulatory restrictions on certain activities, credit default swap regulations, and mandatory filing of security interests in CERSAI, supplemented by requirements for borrower Legal Entity Identifiers. These consolidated directions effective immediately replace previous guidelines and empower NBFCs to strengthen credit risk governance while enabling RBI to monitor systemic risks arising from interconnected financial intermediaries.

The RBI's Small Finance Banks Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025 establish comprehensive prudential framework for SFBs to manage credit risk through board-approved policies, statutory/regulatory restrictions, and oversight mechanisms covering areas such as country risk, unhedged foreign currency exposure, borrower LEI requirements, and property valuation standards. The directions apply immediately to all SFBs and mandate compliance across multiple operational areas including credit evaluation, loan systems, security interest filing in CERSAI, and maintenance of cash credit and current accounts with prescribed risk management practices. Key requirements include adherence to regulatory caps on lending to related parties, mandatory use of empaneled valuers for property assessments, and implementation of loan systems for credit delivery while maintaining statutory restrictions on certain high-risk activities and exposures.

The framework also provides protections for dissenting shareholders and establishes norms for promoter share transactions, ensuring orderly consolidation within the payments banking sector while safeguarding stakeholder interests and regulatory compliance.

# RBI Directions on Regional Rural Banks – Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters (2025)

These Directions establish a transparent, non-discriminatory procedure for RRBs to classify borrowers as wilful defaulters and report them to Credit Information Companies, ensuring other lenders are cautioned against extending further credit to such entities. The framework applies to all Regional Rural Banks and covers treatment of wilful defaulters (those deliberately defaulting with intent or recklessness) and large defaulters (outstanding amounts of ₹1 crore and above), with specific provisions on fund diversion, guarantor obligations, and director accountability. RRBs must adhere to principles of natural justice in classification, maintain identification committees for oversight, implement preventive measures through enhanced auditor roles, and submit regular reports to RBI in prescribed formats for credit dissemination purposes.

# RBI Master Direction Summary - Currency Chest Reporting Penalties

Banks with Currency Chests must report all transactions (minimum ₹1,00,000, then multiples of ₹50,000) on the same day by 7 pm through the CyM-CC portal, with penal interest levied on the "amount due" for delays or incorrect reporting calculated on a T+0 basis. Ineligible cash amounts (held outside vaults, lacking CCTV coverage, or under unauthorized locks) included in chest balances are treated as wrong reporting and attract penal interest from inclusion until exclusion date. Additional penalties include ₹50,000 for wrongly reporting soiled note remittances as withdrawals, with penal interest rates specified in paragraph 4 of the circular.

# RBI Rural Co-operative Banks KYC Directions 2025 Summary

These directions establish comprehensive Know Your Customer (KYC), Customer Due Diligence (CDD), and Anti-Money Laundering/Counter-Terrorist Financing (AML/CFT) requirements applicable to State and Central Co-operative Banks under the Rural Cooperative Banking framework. Rural co-operative banks must implement robust customer acceptance policies, risk management procedures, customer identification processes, and enhanced due diligence measures aligned with FATF standards and India's Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002. The directions mandate ongoing customer monitoring, proper record maintenance, and mandatory reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU)-India, with requirements for beneficial owner identification and enhanced scrutiny for high-risk customers to prevent misuse of the banking system for money laundering and terrorist financing.

The amendment modifies asset classification and provisioning norms for commercial banks implementing resolution plans under Chapter VI-A of the stressed assets framework, allowing accounts to be retained or upgraded to 'Standard' status upon plan implementation while subsequent classification follows standard criteria. Banks must maintain an additional 5% specific provision on outstanding debt for resolution plans and repeated restructuring (capped at 100%), with provisions reversible upon 20% debt repayment without further defaults or restructuring, or after one year for non-fund-based facilities without default. Interest income recognition shifts to accrual basis for resolved accounts under the framework, while accounts with repeated restructuring use cash basis recognition, with all amendments effective July 1, 2026.

The RBI amended capital adequacy norms for Payments Banks to allow quarterly inclusion of profits in Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital calculation, effective immediately. Eligible profits must be calculated using a formula that deducts 25% of average dividends from three prior years, with quarterly financial statements requiring audit or limited review, and cumulative net losses fully deducted from CET1. This modification enables Payments Banks more flexibility in maintaining capital adequacy ratios (CRAR) by recognizing current-year earnings on a quarterly basis while ensuring conservative treatment of dividend distributions.

# RBI Circular Summary: Regional Rural Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend, 2026

These Directions, effective FY 2026-27, establish prudential norms for Regional Rural Banks to declare dividends only when they meet strict eligibility criteria including maintaining regulatory capital compliance, achieving positive adjusted Profit After Tax (after deducting 50% of Net NPAs), and having no explicit RBI restrictions. Dividend payments are capped at 80% of adjusted PAT with a tiered structure based on Tier 1 Capital Ratios, ranging from 0% payout for ratios up to 7% to 100% for ratios above 19%, with Board oversight requiring consideration of NPA divergences, auditor reports, capital positions, and long-term growth plans. Extraordinary profits and profits overstated in audit reports are ineligible for dividend distribution, and non-compliance will attract penal consequences.

# Summary of RBI Regional Rural Banks Concentration Risk Management Directions, 2025

Regional Rural Banks must now adhere to strict prudential exposure limits on concentrations to single borrowers and group borrowers, with these limits defined as percentages of "owned funds" (paid-up capital, statutory reserves, and free reserves, excluding provisions and accumulated losses). The Directions establish that exposures include both funded and non-funded credit limits, sanctioned limits or outstanding amounts (whichever is higher), and investment exposures, requiring RRBs to develop comprehensive written loan policies with explicit counterparty and sectoral exposure limits. These regulations came into immediate effect on November 28, 2025, building upon prudential frameworks originally introduced in 1995 and revised subsequently, to mitigate concentration risk and protect the banking system from counterparty defaults.

The RBI's 2025 Master Directions on Commercial Banks' Credit Risk Transfer establish a comprehensive regulatory framework governing loan transfers, co-lending arrangements, and inter-bank participations, effective immediately for most provisions and January 1, 2026 for co-lending arrangements. Banks can only transfer or acquire loans through specified mechanisms and must comply with prudential norms regarding stressed vs. non-stressed loan transfers, with overseas branches permitted to transfer both performing and non-performing exposures to regulated entities in host jurisdictions. The directions aim to develop India's credit risk transfer market while maintaining financial stability, requiring banks to adhere to strict conditions on borrower consent, risk retention, and documentation for all credit risk distribution arrangements.

These RBI Directions establish a comprehensive regulatory framework for securitisation transactions by Small Finance Banks (SFBs), permitting them to participate only as originators and providers of credit enhancements and liquidity supports, not as investors. The Directions mandate stringent requirements including minimum retention requirements, origination standards, bankruptcy-remote special purpose entities, comprehensive disclosure norms, and capital requirements for securitisation exposures to ensure financial stability and transparency. The framework emphasizes simple, transparent, and comparable (STC) securitisations while restricting SFBs from investor participation, thereby limiting their market role and protecting against systemic risks associated with complex securitisation structures.

# RBI Rural Co-operative Banks Financial Statements Directions 2025 Summary

This circular establishes mandatory financial statement presentation and disclosure requirements for Rural Co-operative Banks (State and Central Co-operative Banks) under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, effective from the notification date. Rural Co-operative Banks must prepare Balance Sheets and Profit & Loss Accounts in the prescribed Third Schedule format, comply with all applicable Accounting Standards as Level I enterprises per ICAI guidelines, and adhere to RBI-specific guidance on standards like AS-5 regarding prior period items and materiality thresholds. The directions cover critical areas including balance sheet format, notes to accounts, disclosure requirements, inter-branch provisioning, nostro account reconciliation, reserve fund transfers, fraud provisioning, and specific accounting treatments to ensure uniform and transparent financial reporting across the cooperative banking sector.

Urban Co-operative Banks must establish board-approved policies and governance frameworks for outsourcing financial services and IT services, with mandatory compliance for IT outsourcing agreements by April 10, 2026 or upon renewal, whichever is earlier. The directions apply to all Urban Co-operative Banks for financial services outsourcing, but IT-specific requirements (Chapter IV) apply only to Tier-3 and Tier-4 banks and include strict risk management, confidentiality, security, and business continuity provisions. Banks are prohibited from outsourcing certain critical functions, must maintain oversight and accountability, ensure service provider evaluation and monitoring, implement exit strategies, and establish grievance redressal mechanisms for outsourced services.

# RBI Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Second Amendment Directions, 2026

The RBI has amended the 2025 Directions to harmonize prudential norms for resolution plans of exposures affected by natural calamities (defined as events recognized under NDRF/SDRF or external events like riots causing economic loss). Banks must now incorporate board-approved policies with objective principles for relief measures, potential relief measures with verifiable parameters, and delegation matrices for timely implementation, while Part E of Chapter VI on Special Cases of Restructuring has been deleted. New Chapter VI-A establishes a framework where State/Union Territory Level Bankers' Committees or District Consultative Committees must convene within 15 days of a calamity declaration to assess impact severity, identify affected borrowers, and determine moratorium periods, with decisions communicated to all committee members and RBI Regional Offices.

# RBI Commercial Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services Directions, 2025 Summary

The RBI Directions establish comprehensive regulatory framework for commercial banks to undertake various financial services including equipment leasing, factoring, mutual funds, insurance, pension fund management, investment advisory, portfolio management, broking, and agency businesses, with Board-approved policies and prudential guidelines mandatory for each activity. Banks must operate through properly structured subsidiaries or direct undertakings, maintain appropriate risk management frameworks, and adhere to specific application procedures for each financial service, while non-banking financial company group entities are also subject to certain provisions regarding risk participation and regulatory compliance. The Directions apply immediately to all commercial banks (excluding Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks) and establish clear governance structures requiring Board oversight, conflict of interest management, and compliance with both RBI regulations and other applicable laws governing individual financial services.

This Amendment Directions modifies income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning norms for All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) implementing resolution plans under the stressed asset resolution framework effective July 1, 2026. Key provisions include: borrower accounts implementing resolution plans may retain 'Standard' classification or be upgraded from NPA to 'Standard', while accounts undergoing repeated restructuring continue as 'Standard'; AIFIs must maintain additional specific provisions of 5% of outstanding debt for each resolution plan implementation or restructuring instance, reversible only upon 20% debt repayment without subsequent default or restructuring; and interest income recognition switches to accrual basis for initial resolution plans but reverts to cash basis for repeatedly restructured accounts. These amendments aim to facilitate stressed asset resolution while ensuring prudential safeguards through enhanced provisioning and stricter income recognition criteria for accounts requiring multiple restructurings.

The RBI has issued mandatory Directions for Rural Co-operative Banks (State and Central Co-operative Banks) to manage concentration risk in their lending portfolios through uniform exposure norms applicable to both individual and corporate borrowers. Key requirements include establishing Board-approved policies for individual lending and Commercial Real Estate-Residential Housing financing, with capital fund and lendable resources serving as the baseline for calculating exposure limits. Non-compliance with these Directions will trigger supervisory and enforcement actions against RCBs, strengthening prudential risk management across the cooperative banking sector.

The RBI's Rural Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 (effective November 28, 2025) establish a comprehensive regulatory framework for all State and Central Co-operative Banks operating in India, covering institutional governance, customer service standards, financial inclusion, payment services, deposit accounts, and responsible lending practices. Key requirements include implementing institutional frameworks for responsible business conduct, maintaining customer service standards in branches, protecting customer interests through guidance and disclosure, ensuring financial accessibility, and adhering to responsible lending norms with standardized definitions for consumer credit and other banking terms. The directions will impact rural co-operative banks' operations by mandating enhanced customer protections, standardized processes for deposit account settlements and safe deposit locker management, transparent fee structures, and responsible lending conduct aligned with RBI's broader financial inclusion objectives.

These Directions establish a comprehensive Asset Liability Management (ALM) framework for five All India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID), effective immediately from November 28, 2025. The Board of each institution must assume overall responsibility for managing liquidity risk, interest rate risk, currency risk, and equity price risk, with oversight delegated to a Management Committee or ALCO that implements and periodically reviews ALM policies and limits. AIFIs are required to prepare regulatory statements on liquidity risk and interest rate sensitivity, adopt stress testing and modern risk measurement techniques when technically capable, and maintain internal prudential limits for cumulative negative liquidity gaps, with specific reporting requirements to RBI at defined frequencies.

The RBI's 2025 Directions establish mandatory authentication standards for all digital payment transactions in India, requiring at least two distinct factors of authentication (with at least one being dynamic) to be implemented by all Payment System Providers and Participants by April 1, 2026. These directions replace the previous reliance on SMS-based OTP as the sole additional factor and enable the payments ecosystem to adopt alternative authentication mechanisms such as biometrics, software tokens, and device-native authentication while maintaining security. The requirements apply to domestic digital payment transactions and specific cross-border card transactions, with certain exemptions listed in Annexure-1, and place responsibility on issuers to ensure compliance through robust, interoperable, and risk-based authentication approaches.

These Directions establish a transparent, non-discriminatory procedure for commercial banks to classify borrowers as wilful defaulters while ensuring compliance with natural justice principles, applicable to all scheduled commercial banks except SFBs, LABs, PBs, and RRBs. Banks must report wilful defaulters and large defaulters to Credit Information Companies, with restrictions on further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters applied across all RBI-regulated entities regardless of lender status. The Directions define key concepts including diversion of funds, default classification, and establish an identification committee framework to oversee the classification process with standardized reporting formats.

The Reserve Bank of India's Small Finance Banks Directions, 2025 establish comprehensive prudential norms for income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning of advances to ensure consistency and transparency in financial reporting and align with international best practices. The directions mandate specific classification criteria for non-performing assets (NPAs), with provisions ranging from standard to loss assets, along with detailed rules for income reversal and recovery appropriation upon NPA classification. Small Finance Banks must also comply with additional guidelines for restructured accounts under the complementary Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, and maintain documented policies on lending prudence, consumer education, and disclosure requirements enforced by their boards.

This RBI Amendment Direction, effective immediately as of April 27, 2026, modifies the Rural Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services Directions 2025 by adding "AgriSURE - Agri Fund for Start Ups & Rural Enterprises" to Annex I of permissible financial services. The amendment, issued under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949, expands the scope of financial services that rural co-operative banks are authorized to undertake in support of agricultural entrepreneurship. This broadens the regulatory framework for rural cooperative banks to facilitate agricultural start-ups and rural enterprise development through the AgriSURE scheme.

These Directions mandate that All India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, NaBFID, NHB, and SIDBI) establish board-approved outsourcing policies with robust governance frameworks for managing IT service outsourcing risks, including evaluation of service providers, security controls, and business continuity planning. Existing IT outsourcing agreements must comply with these provisions by April 10, 2026, or upon renewal (whichever is earlier), while new agreements must comply immediately upon execution. The Directions comprehensively regulate material IT outsourcing across infrastructure management, cloud services, security operations, offshore arrangements, and payment systems, with specific requirements for confidentiality, monitoring, exit strategies, and grievance redressal mechanisms.

# RBI Master Direction on Payment Aggregator Regulation Summary

The RBI has issued a comprehensive Master Direction (effective immediately) consolidating and rationalizing previous guidelines on Payment Aggregators (PAs), extending regulatory framework to cover physical point-of-sale operations and cross-border transactions under unified rules. The direction applies to all bank and non-bank entities operating as PAs, as well as Acquiring Banks and Scheduled Commercial Banks, with requirements covering authorization, capital standards, governance, dispute management, KYC/due diligence, fraud prevention, and mandatory escrow account arrangements for fund settlement. Key provisions include stringent security and risk management frameworks, merchant due diligence through contact point verification, core escrow account maintenance, and specific compliance obligations for cross-border PAs, strengthening consumer protection and payment system stability.

The RBI has issued comprehensive directions for Core Investment Companies (CICs) effective November 28, 2025, establishing regulatory requirements for non-banking financial companies that invest primarily in group company equities and securities, with at least 90% of net assets in such investments and at least 60% in equity shares or InvIT holdings. CICs are subject to capital requirements, prudential regulations, corporate governance standards, risk management frameworks, and mandatory disclosure requirements while restricted from trading investments (except strategic block sales), carrying on other financial activities beyond specified group lending and guarantees, or holding non-financial assets exceeding 10% of net assets. The directions apply to registered CICs with compliance requirements across board governance, shareholding patterns, overseas investments, and quarterly/annual reporting to the RBI, with unregistered CICs exempted from applicability.

# Summary of RBI Non-Banking Financial Companies - Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026

These Directions establish a mandatory Internal Ombudsman framework for eligible NBFCs (deposit-taking NBFCs with 10+ branches and non-deposit-taking NBFCs with ₹5,000 crore+ assets and public customer interface) to strengthen internal grievance redressal and ensure independent review of customer complaints before rejection. The framework, effective immediately except for certain implementation clauses due by June 30, 2026, designates an apex-level Internal Ombudsman and Deputy Internal Ombudsman as "Competent Authority" to review complaints alleging service deficiencies and provide speedy resolution. The directions apply to specified categories of NBFCs while excluding housing finance companies, core investment companies, and entities under insolvency or liquidation, with new eligible NBFCs having six months from meeting criteria to implement compliance.

The Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) allows resident individuals to remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year for permitted current or capital account transactions, with the limit revised periodically based on macroeconomic conditions since its introduction in 2004. The scheme is available only to resident individuals (including minors with guardian countersignature) and excludes corporates, partnership firms, HUFs, and trusts, with permissible transactions including foreign bank account opening, overseas investments, and immovable property acquisition. Authorised Dealers must ensure compliance with FEMA regulations, prohibit margin-related remittances and non-permitted transactions, and restrict family clubbing for capital account transactions unless members are co-owners/partners, with detailed reporting requirements specified in the Master Direction on Reporting.

# Summary of RBI Small Finance Banks Concentration Risk Management Directions, 2025

Small Finance Banks must adhere to prudential exposure limits on single and group borrowers as a percentage of capital funds (Tier I and Tier II capital), with exposure calculated as the higher of sanctioned limits or outstanding amounts across credit, investment, and derivative products to mitigate concentration risk. The Board must establish robust risk management frameworks and oversight mechanisms to monitor concentration exposures, while banks are prohibited from exceeding exposure ceilings in anticipation of future capital infusions. These directions apply immediately to all Small Finance Banks and establish comprehensive guidelines for managing asset-side concentration risk, liability-side inter-bank exposures, sectoral diversification, and country risk exposures.

These Directions establish comprehensive guidelines for Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) regarding the classification, valuation, and operation of their investment portfolios, effective from November 28, 2025. UCBs must classify investments into three categories (Held to Maturity, Held for Trading, and Available for Sale), maintain appropriate valuation methods for each category, and adhere to prudential limits on non-SLR securities and interbank deposits. The framework mandates robust internal controls, Board oversight of investment policies, income recognition standards, and provisioning requirements while ensuring compliance with RBI's regulatory requirements for investment operations in government and non-SLR securities.

These Directions establish a comprehensive framework for Small Finance Banks to regulate interest rates on all deposit categories including domestic rupee deposits, non-resident rupee deposits, and foreign currency deposits, effective from the date of publication on the RBI website. The framework defines key deposit types (current accounts, savings deposits, term deposits, bulk deposits, and floating rate deposits) and specifies requirements for interest calculation, payment periodicity, premature withdrawal penalties, and treatment of deceased depositors' accounts. Small Finance Banks must comply with prohibited practices outlined in Chapter VI while following the prescribed interest rate guidelines across all deposit schemes, including special provisions for farmers' composite cash credit accounts and non-resident Indian deposits.

The RBI's 2025 Directions establish prudential norms for Rural Co-operative Banks (State and Central Co-operative Banks) to declare dividends, requiring compliance with capital adequacy ratios, Net Non-Performing Asset ratios ≤5%, CRR/SLR requirements, and full provisioning for impaired assets before dividend payment. RCBs must declare dividends exclusively from net profit after statutory provisions and accumulated loss adjustments, with Board consideration of current and projected capital positions against applicable requirements and economic outlook. The Directions, effective immediately, repeal previous dividend-related guidelines while preserving all prior actions, approvals, and legal proceedings under the superseded framework.

The RBI repeals the Commercial Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions of 2025, effective April 1, 2027, and replaces them with updated 2026 Directions to modernize regulatory frameworks for asset management and provisioning standards. All actions, approvals, and obligations initiated under the repealed 2025 Directions remain valid and enforceable, ensuring continuity in compliance and regulatory oversight. The repeal does not affect any existing rights, liabilities, penalties, or ongoing investigations, which continue to be governed by the previous framework.

# RBI Small Finance Banks Climate Finance Directions, 2025 Summary

Small Finance Banks must establish Board-approved policies for accepting "green deposits" (deposits earmarked for green financing) and implement comprehensive frameworks for managing climate change risks, with strict requirements to prevent greenwashing and ensure proceeds finance only eligible green activities/projects. Green deposits must be denominated in Indian Rupees with tenor and interest rates compliant with RBI's deposit directions, and banks must conduct third-party verification, impact assessments, and detailed reporting on green finance allocation. The directions take immediate effect and require banks raising green deposits to finance green activities only prospectively (not retroactively) while establishing governance mechanisms with Board oversight and periodic review reports to ensure environmental and depositor protection.

The RBI amended the Rural Co-operative Banks Governance Directions to address directors circumventing tenure limits by resigning briefly and returning within short periods, thereby extending their tenure beyond the statutory maximum of ten years. The amendment mandates a mandatory three-year cooling-off period after directors complete ten continuous years of service before they can be re-appointed to the same RCB's board, during which they cannot be associated with the bank except as a member or customer. The regulation includes an explanation clarifying that continuous tenure calculations include periods separated by interruptions of less than three years, but exclude periods after interruptions of at least three years, and takes effect immediately upon issuance.

These directions establish critical regulatory requirements covering board governance, asset reconstruction procedures, securitisation guidelines, capital adequacy norms, and accounting standards to ensure prudent and efficient functioning of ARCs in India's financial system. ARCs must comply with provisions regarding Net Owned Fund (NOF) calculations, Non-Performing Asset (NPA) classification (assets with 180+ days overdue amounts), and restrictions on investments in group companies and subsidiaries to maintain financial stability.

These Directions apply to all NOFHCs as defined and impose capital adequacy, exposure limits, and regulatory oversight obligations on a stand-alone and consolidated basis to ensure financial stability and protect banking system integrity.

These 2025 directions, effective immediately, supersede previous regulations and establish the framework for RRBs' reserve maintenance and statutory reporting obligations to the RBI.

The Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 establish regulatory framework for UCBs to open branches, extension counters, ATMs, and engage business correspondents/facilitators through both automatic and prior approval routes, with specific eligibility criteria and area-of-operation restrictions. Urban Co-operative Banks must adopt Board-approved policies governing branch expansion based on financial viability, engagement of intermediaries with oversight mechanisms, and doorstep banking services to ensure customer protection and regulatory compliance. General provisions on standard assets (Stage 1/2) and excess provisions from NPA sales now qualify for Tier 2 capital up to a maximum of 1.25% of total credit risk-weighted assets, with banks given the option to either net floating provisions against gross NPAs or include them in Tier 2 capital. These amendments, effective April 1, 2027, also delete provisions related to specific exclusions and certain computational methodologies, streamlining the regulatory framework for capital adequacy compliance.

# Digital Payments – E-mandate Framework, 2026 Summary

The RBI has consolidated all e-mandate circulars into a unified framework effective immediately, establishing mandatory requirements for all Payment System Providers and Participants handling recurring transactions via cards, PPI, and UPI. Key provisions include: mandatory additional factor of authentication (AFA) for registration and modifications; pre-transaction notifications at least 24 hours before debit with opt-out functionality; and transaction limits of ₹15,000 without AFA (₹1,00,000 for insurance premiums, mutual funds, and credit card payments). The framework mandates post-transaction notifications, customer-controlled validity periods, and dispute redressal systems while applying RBI's liability protections for unauthorized transactions to e-mandate recurring payments.

The Directions mandate robust transaction monitoring, record maintenance, reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India, and compliance with international agreements, with specific provisions for high-risk customers and enhanced due diligence measures to prevent financial system misuse.

The RBI's Master Directions 2025 mandate that commercial banks prepare standardized Balance Sheets and Profit & Loss accounts in prescribed formats under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, with strict compliance to Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, as amended by RBI guidelines. The directions apply to all commercial banks in India (excluding Regional Rural Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks) and require detailed notes and disclosures covering capital structure, provisioning for fraudes and deferred taxes, nostro account reconciliation, and window dressing controls. These regulations ensure uniform financial reporting, enhanced transparency, and regulatory oversight to maintain banking sector stability and protect depositor interests.
