These Directions establish a non-discriminatory, transparent procedure for NBFCs (NBFC-Middle Layer and above) to classify borrowers as wilful defaulters while adhering to natural justice principles, and mandate dissemination of credit information about such defaulters to prevent further institutional financing. Banks must follow these directions while adhering to more stringent requirements under State Co-operative Societies Acts and other statutory enactments to ensure greater consistency, transparency, and alignment with international prudential practices in their published accounts.

# Summary: Master Direction - Remittance of Assets

This Master Direction consolidates RBI's instructions governing remittance of assets outside India by both residents and non-residents, authorized under Section 47 of FEMA 1999 and regulated through FEMA Notification 13/2016-RB dated April 1, 2016. Authorised Dealer Category-I banks must implement specific procedures for processing asset remittances including funds from deposits, insurance policies, securities sale proceeds, and immovable property held in India. Key beneficiaries include NRIs, PIOs, and certain foreign nationals meeting specific criteria (retired employees, heirs, non-resident widows/widowers), with remittances generally capped at USD 1 million per financial year, subject to applicable regulations and periodic RBI amendments issued via A.P. (DIR Series) Circulars.

The RBI has updated its Master Direction on compounding of FEMA contraventions under the new Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2024, which replaces the 2000 rules and supersedes previous guidance issued in April 2025. The compounding mechanism allows persons to voluntarily resolve FEMA violations (except those under Section 3(a)) within 180 days through RBI-prescribed officers, with penalty amounts up to three times the sum involved or up to Rs. 2 lakhs for non-quantifiable violations. Authorized Dealers must ensure robust internal controls to prevent FEMA contraventions and must inform constituents of the new compounding guidelines, while RBI retains authority to impose additional penalties for non-compliance with directions or filing failures.

# RBI Certificate of Deposit Directions 2021 - Summary

This Master Direction, effective June 7, 2021, supersedes previous CD regulations and governs the issuance and trading of Certificates of Deposit as negotiable, unsecured money market instruments by eligible entities (Scheduled Commercial Banks, Regional Rural Banks, and Small Finance Banks) with maturity periods up to one year. The Directions establish comprehensive definitions, eligibility criteria, and operational frameworks for CD issuance, including settlement mechanisms (Delivery versus Payment), trading on electronic platforms and OTC markets, and compliance requirements for all market participants. Key updates from public feedback reflect RBI's intent to facilitate greater flexibility in liquidity management for CD issuers while maintaining market integrity and regulatory oversight.

# Summary of RBI Directions on Regional Rural Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation, 2025

These Directions, effective January 1, 2026, establish the regulatory framework for Regional Rural Banks to offer digital banking services through internet banking, mobile banking, and other digital channels, with two service tiers: view-only facilities (limited to account viewing and inquiries) and transactional facilities (enabling fund transfers and other value-altering transactions). Banks must implement Core Banking Solutions and IPv6-capable IT infrastructure to provide these services and establish comprehensive policies addressing statutory, regulatory, liquidity, and operational risk management requirements. Banks launching view-only services must notify the RBI's Department of Regulation within 30 days of board approval, accompanied by a Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy report, with copies forwarded to NABARD for supervisory scrutiny.

# RBI Credit and Debit Cards Directions, 2025 - Summary

These Directions, effective immediately, establish comprehensive regulatory guidelines for credit and debit card issuance and conduct by commercial banks in India, excluding Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks. The regulations cover credit card business conduct, debit card issuance, form factors, co-branding arrangements, and define key terms including credit limits, billing cycles, card types (charge cards, corporate cards, co-branded cards), and cardholder protections such as interest-free credit periods and convenience fees. Banks must comply with these Directions alongside existing prudential, payment, and cybersecurity-related RBI directives, establishing standardized requirements for card product features, loyalty programs, and consumer safeguards across the banking sector.

# Summary of RBI Master Directions on Regional Rural Banks – Responsible Business Conduct (2025)

These Directions consolidate RBI's regulatory instructions on customer service and conduct standards specifically for Regional Rural Banks, effective immediately upon issuance and applicable to all RRBs across India. The document establishes comprehensive frameworks across ten chapters covering institutional governance, branch customer service, financial inclusion, deposit management, responsible lending, and payment services, supported by detailed annexures including forms, settlement procedures, and key facts statements. Key provisions define critical terms such as Annual Percentage Rate (APR), Consumer Credit, Bank-induced transactions, and survivorship clauses in accounts, while mandating RRBs to ensure fair customer treatment, transparent disclosure of charges, and protection mechanisms for deposits and safe deposit lockers.

# RBI Master Direction - Overseas Investment Summary

This Master Direction consolidates RBI instructions governing overseas investments by persons resident in India under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules and Regulations, 2022, and applies to all Authorised Dealer Category-I banks facilitating such investments. The framework establishes procedures for obtaining Central Government and RBI approvals, sets pricing guidelines, defines permissible foreign entities (replacing the JV/WOS framework), and mandates compliance with reporting requirements specified in Master Direction 18. Banks must ensure customers comply with financial commitment limits, transfer/liquidation rules, and prohibitions while facilitating remittances and documenting approvals from lenders or investigative agencies as necessary.

# RBI Urban Co-operative Banks Directions 2025 Summary

The Reserve Bank of India has issued prudential directions for Urban Co-operative Banks effective immediately, establishing standardized norms for income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning of advances in alignment with international practices and previous committee recommendations. The directions define key classifications including non-performing assets (NPAs), doubtful assets (those in substandard category for 12+ months), and loss assets, with specific criteria for determining "out of order" status for cash credit/overdraft accounts based on 90-day thresholds. Banks must comply with these directions alongside state cooperative societies acts where more stringent, and apply additional guidelines for restructured accounts as per the RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions 2025.

The RBI's 2025 Directions establish comprehensive governance and risk management requirements for Small Finance Banks outsourcing financial services and IT functions, including mandatory board-approved policies, service provider evaluation frameworks, and strict oversight mechanisms. Banks must ensure outsourced activities comply with confidentiality and security standards, maintain business continuity plans, and implement grievance redressal mechanisms, with existing IT agreements required to comply by April 10, 2026 and new agreements from their effective date. The Directions prohibit outsourcing of certain core banking functions and require prior bank approval for any subcontracting arrangements, while exempting non-banking services like catering and housekeeping from these requirements.

These Master Directions establish a comprehensive framework for scheduled commercial banks and select financial institutions to detect, classify, and report frauds to the RBI under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Banks must implement robust fraud prevention policies with CEO and Board oversight, including quarterly and annual fraud reviews, early warning systems for loan fraud detection, and prompt reporting to the Central Fraud Registry and law enforcement agencies. The directions mandate staff accountability measures, legal audits of large loan accounts, and incentivize early fraud detection while requiring monthly fraud certificates and adherence to specified precautions for cheque-related and consortium lending frauds.

# RBI Circular Summary: Payment Banks Dividend Declaration Directions 2026

The RBI has established prudential norms for Payment Banks to declare dividends, effective FY 2026-27, requiring banks to meet strict eligibility criteria including maintaining regulatory capital compliance, possessing positive adjusted PAT (after deducting 50% of Net NPAs), and remaining free from RBI restrictions on dividend declarations. Dividend payout is capped at 75% of adjusted PAT, with the actual permissible percentage determined by Tier 1 Capital Ratio buckets ranging from 0% (for ratios up to 7.5%) to 100% (for ratios above 19.5%), and banks must ensure capital levels do not fall below regulatory requirements post-dividend payment. Board oversight requires consideration of NPA divergence trends, auditor reports, capital position projections, and long-term growth plans, with non-compliance attracting penal consequences.

Regional Rural Banks must establish board-approved internal principles to ensure interest rates, including all charges, are not usurious and conform to banking norms, with monthly rests for interest charging except for agricultural advances which follow existing crop-linked practices. For microfinance loans, RBs must implement documented interest rate models with transparent component delineation (cost of funds, risk premium, margin) and impose board-approved ceilings on all-inclusive rates subject to RBI supervisory review. Small value loans require prior-approval processes incorporating borrower cash flow analysis, risk-based pricing with security consideration, and published ceilings ensuring total borrower costs are justifiable relative to the bank's lending expenses and expected returns.

These Directions, applicable to five All-India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID), mandate strict compliance with Accounting Standards under Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, and require preparation of both standalone and Consolidated Financial Statements in accordance with AS 21 and related standards. AIFIs must consolidate all domestic and foreign subsidiaries except those specifically permitted exclusions under AS 21, with disclosed reasons for any exclusions, and ensure uniform accounting policies and same reporting dates across consolidated entities. The Directions establish comprehensive requirements for financial statement presentation, disclosure of notes to accounts, and Consolidated Prudential Reporting (CPR), effective immediately.

# RBI Circular Summary: Urban Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters Directions, 2025

These Directions establish a transparent, non-discriminatory procedure for Urban Co-operative Banks to classify borrowers as wilful defaulters based on natural justice principles, with immediate applicability to Scheduled and non-Scheduled UCBs (Tier 3 and 4). UCBs must report wilful defaulters and large defaulters to Credit Information Companies to prevent further institutional finance, with restrictions on financial accommodation applying across all RBI-regulated entities including Tier 1 and 2 UCBs. Key definitions include credit facilities (fund and non-fund-based), default classification per stress resolution directions, diversion of funds covering misappropriation and unauthorized deployment, and associated directors, establishing comprehensive governance for defaulter identification and credit information dissemination.

The RBI's Commercial Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation Directions, 2025 establish a regulatory framework for voluntary mergers between commercial banks and with certain non-bank financial entities (SFBs, LABs, PBs, NBFCs), effective immediately. Amalgamation decisions require approval from a two-thirds majority of board members from both merging entities, with boards mandated to conduct due diligence, validate swap ratios through independent valuers, and ensure compliance with RBI governance and shareholding guidelines. The directions define the roles of amalgamating and amalgamated entities, provide for dissenting shareholder protections, regulate promoter share transactions, and require RBI sanction before implementation under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

This document is a Money Market Operations press release from May 25, 2026, not a regulatory circular. It reports daily liquidity management data showing zero overnight money market activity, RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility operations injecting ₹112 crore through fixed-rate repo at 5.50%, and a net liquidity absorption of ₹55,286.42 crore across all outstanding operations. Scheduled Commercial Banks held ₹7,90,353 crore in cash reserves against an average daily requirement of ₹7,96,910 crore for the fortnight ending May 31, 2026, indicating a marginal liquidity deficit.

RBI requires financial institutions to submit multiple regulatory returns across different departments and frequencies to monitor banking operations, payment systems, credit activities, and foreign exchange transactions. Key reporting entities include scheduled commercial banks, primary dealers, authorized dealers, and payment service providers, with submission platforms including CIMS, email, and specialized systems like BoP/FETERS. Returns range from fortnightly submissions on monetary aggregates and forex transactions to quarterly/annual filings on credit statistics, deposits, and international banking positions, enabling RBI's comprehensive supervision of the financial system.

# RBI Circular Summary

The RBI issued the Sixth Amendment Directions to the Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025, effective May 18, 2026, in response to amendments made to the Investment Portfolio Classification and Valuation directions. The amendment deletes Sub-paragraph 21(i)(b) from the 2025 Directions, aligning capital adequacy norms with the revised investment portfolio operational framework. This modification ensures consistency between prudential capital requirements and updated investment classification standards for commercial banks.

Banks must examine all banknotes tendered over counters and in bulk using machines and immediately impound any counterfeit notes with a standardized stamp, issuing receipts to tenderers while maintaining separate registers. Banks must report detected counterfeits to police—consolidated monthly reports for up to four notes per transaction, and immediate FIR filings for five or more notes—while designating nodal officers and establishing Forged Notes Vigilance Cells at head offices. Banks failing to impound detected counterfeits face penalties for wilful involvement in circulating counterfeit currency, and must provide staff training and submit regular data reports to RBI, NCRB, and FIU-IND.

The RBI has issued Master Directions on Cyber Resilience and Digital Payment Security Controls for non-bank Payment System Operators (PSOs), effective immediately with phased implementation timelines: large PSOs by April 1, 2025, medium PSOs by April 1, 2026, and small PSOs by April 1, 2028. The directions establish governance controls requiring Board oversight through a dedicated sub-committee, comprehensive baseline security measures across inventory management, network security, data protection, and incident response, alongside specific digital payment security controls for mobile payments, card payments, and prepaid instruments. PSOs must ensure compliance by unregulated entities in their ecosystem (payment gateways, vendors, third-party service providers) through Board-approved organizational policies, with these directions superseding any conflicting existing instructions.

The RBI's Seventh Amendment Directions, 2026 modifies financial statement presentation and disclosure requirements for commercial banks, primarily aligning with the newly issued Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions, 2026. Key changes include: separating provisions for Stage 1 and Stage 2 assets in the balance sheet rather than netting them against gross advances, clarifying interest income recognition across advances and investments with specific reference to regulatory asset classification, and deleting outdated guidance on capitalizing broken period interest on securities acquisitions. The amendment also updates accounting standards to clarify that non-recognition of income for non-performing assets in compliance with RBI regulations shall not be qualified by statutory auditors, and refines provisions on impairment assessments for non-banking assets acquired in settlement of claims.

The RBI amended the 2025 Commercial Banks Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions to align them with the new 2026 Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions, with modifications effective April 27, 2026. Key additions include expanded stress indicators (credit rating downgrades, collateral value changes, fee payment delays, and anticipated covenant breaches) in the definition of stressed assets, and comprehensive updates to provisioning requirements across restructured accounts, insolvency proceedings, natural calamity relief, and NPAs to reference the new 2026 framework. These amendments ensure consistent application of asset classification and provisioning norms across stressed asset resolution mechanisms, strengthening regulatory oversight of banks' credit risk management and capital adequacy.

# RBI Master Directions Summary: Regional Rural Banks Financial Statements 2025

These Directions establish mandatory formats and disclosure requirements for Regional Rural Banks' balance sheets and profit and loss accounts under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, effective immediately. RRBs must comply with Accounting Standards under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, while following prescribed formats and specific instructions for capital, reserves, and asset classification items. The Directions comprehensively govern financial statement presentation, inter-branch provisioning, nostro account reconciliation, fraud provisioning, and deferred tax treatment to ensure standardized and transparent financial reporting across all RRBs.

The Reserve Bank of India has issued comprehensive Master Directions regulating Rupee interest rate derivatives (IRD) transactions in both OTC and recognized stock exchange markets, effective March 1, 2026, superseding previous directions and establishing standardized definitions and frameworks for various derivative instruments including Forward Rate Agreements, Interest Rate Swaps, and Options. The directions apply to all participants in the IRD market and establish requirements for back-to-back arrangements, benchmark interest rate usage, and foreign currency-settled derivatives while clarifying the scope of permissible transactions and participant eligibility. Key provisions include specific definitions of derivative instruments, governance frameworks for Electronic Trading Platforms, and alignment with FEMA regulations for non-resident participation and foreign portfolio investor activities in the derivatives market.

# RBI Master Direction – Import of Goods and Services Summary

This Master Direction (updated January 12, 2026) governs import of goods and services into India under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, laying down modalities for Authorised Dealer Category-I banks to conduct foreign exchange business with importers in compliance with regulatory frameworks. The directive covers general guidelines including remittances, import licenses, settlement timelines, advance remittances, and operational procedures such as letter of credit issuance, import evidence collection, and specialized imports like gold and BPO equipment. AD Category-I banks must ensure imports conform to the Foreign Trade Policy, follow standard banking practices (UCPDC), and maintain compliance with collateral regulations including R&D Cess Act and Income Tax provisions while implementing these directions.

# RBI Master Direction Summary: External Commercial Borrowings and Foreign Currency Transactions

This Master Direction consolidates regulations governing External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) and Trade Credit under FEMA, establishing comprehensive frameworks for eligible borrowers, recognized lenders, maturity prescriptions, cost parameters, and permitted end-uses for overseas borrowing. Authorised Dealer banks are mandated to implement specific operational procedures including loan registration, hedging requirements, security creation mechanisms, and strict debt-equity ratio compliance while monitoring individual borrowing limits and currency specifications. The directive requires continuous reporting through A.P. (DIR Series) Circulars for regulatory updates, with detailed provisions on ECB conversion into equity, parking of proceeds domestically and abroad, and issuance of guarantees by Indian financial institutions to ensure transparent foreign exchange management.

# RBI Regional Rural Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025 Summary

This Master Direction establishes a comprehensive framework for Regional Rural Banks to govern interest rates on all deposit categories, including domestic rupee deposits, non-resident rupee deposits, and foreign currency deposits, effective from November 28, 2025. The directions mandate specific rules for current accounts (non-interest bearing), savings deposits, term deposits (including bulk deposits of ₹1 crore and above), and deposits of deceased depositors, while prescribing penalties for premature withdrawals and defining additional interest payment provisions. RRBs must comply with these regulatory requirements covering interest calculation methods, floating rate mechanisms, deposit classifications, foreign currency account conversions, and prohibited practices to ensure consistent and transparent deposit interest policies across all Regional Rural Banks.

# RBI Local Area Banks Governance Directions 2025 - Summary

These Directions establish comprehensive governance framework for Local Area Banks covering board constitution, director appointments, and remuneration policies, effective immediately under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Banks must conduct mandatory due diligence at appointment/re-appointment of directors based on fit and proper criteria, with scrutiny by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee using standardized declarations to ensure integrity and suitability. The framework introduces regulatory mechanisms including malus and clawback provisions for variable remuneration, defines roles for independent directors and board committees, and requires banks to implement control function standards and material risk taker governance aligned with RBI regulatory objectives.

The RBI Master Direction on Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives (effective November 8, 2024) establishes mandatory requirements for exchange of variation margin and initial margin between eligible market participants on foreign exchange, interest rate, credit, and other specified derivative contracts. The Directions apply to new derivative contracts entered after the effective date, with grandfathered contracts (entered before this date) exempted unless substantially amended, and cover non-centrally cleared derivatives across multiple asset classes to align with international regulatory standards. These comprehensive requirements aim to mitigate counterparty credit risk and enhance financial stability in the derivatives market by standardizing margining practices across different categories of OTC derivatives traded in India.

The Reserve Bank of India has issued Master Directions for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) effective November 28, 2025, establishing comprehensive guidelines for the classification, valuation, and operation of investment portfolios covering three categories: Held to Maturity (HTM), Held for Trading (HFT), and Available for Sale (AFS). The directions mandate that RRBs establish robust internal control systems, maintain prudential limits on non-SLR securities and broker exposures, and engage in government securities trading through approved channels like NDS-OM and primary auctions, while requiring board oversight of investment policies and sponsor bank coordination. RRBs must implement strict provisioning requirements for non-performing investments, maintain an Investment Fluctuation Reserve, recognize income according to specified norms, and ensure compliance with accounting and audit requirements including regular review and reporting mechanisms to the RBI.

# RBI Local Area Banks – Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025

Local Area Banks must establish robust credit risk management frameworks compliant with board-approved policies, statutory restrictions on lending activities, and regulatory prohibitions on related-party transactions to mitigate systemic and idiosyncratic risks. The Directions mandate compliance with prudential tools including restrictions on unhedged foreign currency exposures, mandatory Legal Entity Identifier requirements for borrowers, and standardized valuation procedures for collateral through empaneled valuers. Banks must maintain proper security documentation through CERSAI filing for immovable, movable, and intangible assets, and adhere to specific operational guidelines for cash credit, current accounts, and overdraft facilities to strengthen overall credit discipline.

# Summary

These RBI Directions establish a regulatory framework enabling Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) to undertake specified financial services including marketing of mutual fund units, insurance business as corporate agents, and merchant acquiring business, subject to Board approval and compliance with prescribed guidelines. RRBs are prohibited from investing in Alternative Investment Funds and from undertaking financial services with debtor companies to which they have current or recent loan exposures, ensuring conflict of interest prevention. The Directions come into force with immediate effect and supersede previous frameworks, applying comprehensively to all RRBs while clarifying that RBI's powers remain unbarred by other applicable laws.

This Master Direction governs the export of goods and services from India under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, establishing procedures for realization, repatriation of export proceeds, and maintenance of foreign currency accounts by Authorized Dealer banks. The circular consolidates multiple regulatory provisions and amendments (updated through January 2026) covering export documentation (EDF/SOFTEX forms), special arrangements like counter-trade and project exports, and obligations of authorized dealers regarding advance receipts and account management. # RBI Master Direction - Money Changing Activities Summary

Money changing business in India can only be conducted by RBI-authorized entities under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999; unauthorized operators face penalties, and this Master Direction consolidates all regulations governing Authorized Dealers Category-I, Category-II, and Full Fledged Money Changers (FFMCs). Key operational requirements include strict KYC/AML/CFT compliance, appointment guidelines for agents/franchisees with minimum net owned funds of Rs. 10 lakh, and restrictions on currency sales (only Indian Rupee conversions permitted, except within 10 km of Pakistan/Bangladesh borders with prior approval). All existing franchisee arrangements must be discontinued by May 6, 2028, with no fresh franchisee arrangements permitted henceforth, and the RBI retains authority to issue further directions through A.P. (DIR Series) Circulars regarding operational conduct and regulatory changes.

# RBI Payments Banks CRR and SLR Directions 2025 Summary

These Directions establish mandatory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements for all Payments Banks, effective immediately, with CRR reported via Form A and SLR via Form VIII statutory returns. Payments Banks must maintain specified CRR percentages of aggregate deposits with the RBI and hold approved SLR securities (Government of India dated securities, Treasury Bills, and State Development Loans) as unencumbered assets, with detailed computation and apportionment procedures for savings bank accounts into demand and time liabilities. Non-compliance with these liquidity maintenance requirements is subject to penalties as outlined in Chapter VI, with specific provisions allowing certain encumbered securities (those pledged to RBI for MSF or acquired under LAF/repo) to qualify toward SLR compliance.

# RBI Amendment Directions Summary

These Amendment Directions establish a new Chapter VI-A for resolving stressed assets of All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) affected by natural calamities or external events like riots, with relief measures applicable only upon formal government declaration of such calamities. AIFIs must incorporate board-approved policies with specific relief objectives, parameters, and delegation matrices for timely implementation of restructuring and additional financing measures. State Level Bankers' Committees (SLBC) and District Consultative Committees (DCC) must convene within 15 days of calamity declaration to assess impact severity and formulate objective criteria for identifying affected borrowers and determining moratorium periods.

These Directions establish comprehensive Know Your Customer (KYC) requirements for Urban Co-operative Banks to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing, aligned with India's obligations under international standards set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). The regulations mandate strict customer acceptance policies, customer identification procedures, and customer due diligence measures across all customer categories including individuals, sole proprietorships, and legal entities. Urban Co-operative Banks must implement enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers, maintain detailed records, conduct ongoing monitoring, and report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India in compliance with the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 and related rules.

# RBI Circular Summary: Regional Rural Banks – Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025

These Directions establish prudential capital adequacy norms for Regional Rural Banks, requiring them to maintain a minimum Capital to Risk Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 9 percent on an ongoing basis, with regulatory capital comprising Tier 1 capital (paid-up share capital, reserves, and revaluation reserves at 55% discount) and Tier 2 capital. The Directions define key components of regulatory capital, prescribe computation of Risk Weighted Assets, and outline regulatory adjustments and deductions applicable to RRBs for ensuring financial stability and resilience. These Directions come into effect immediately and supersede previous capital adequacy frameworks for RRBs, requiring compliance with specific reporting and disclosure requirements as outlined in the accompanying annexes.

# RBI Payments Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing Directions, 2025 Summary

These directions, effective immediately, establish comprehensive governance and risk management requirements for payments banks outsourcing financial services and IT services, with existing IT agreements required to comply by April 10, 2026, and new agreements immediately. Key restrictions include prohibiting outsourcing of board-level functions, audit services, and statutory compliance responsibilities, while requiring board-approved outsourcing policies, rigorous service provider evaluation, secure data handling, business continuity plans, and grievance redressal mechanisms for outsourced activities. The directions apply to all outsourcing arrangements with group entities or unrelated third parties, both domestic and offshore, excluding routine non-banking services, and impose mandatory monitoring, exit strategies for IT services, and compliance with data security and confidentiality standards.

The RBI has amended the Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies (NOFHC) Directions 2025 to align prudential norms for income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning of advances with the newly issued Commercial Banks Directions 2026. The amendment modifies paragraph 20 of the NOFHC Directions to incorporate these updated prudential standards, effective April 1, 2027. This change ensures consistency in regulatory requirements across financial holding companies and commercial banks regarding advance management and financial stability.

This RBI amendment modifies paragraph 131 of the Commercial Banks - Concentration Risk Management Directions, 2025, requiring banks to reference country risk classifications published by the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Limited (ECGC) for concentration risk assessment purposes. The amendment comes into force on April 01, 2027, providing banks with a standardized framework for evaluating sovereign and country-specific risks in their lending portfolios. This change aligns concentration risk management with the updated Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2026, ensuring consistency in risk assessment methodologies across RBI's regulatory framework.

Regulated entities must comply with Section 51A of UAPA, 1967 by ensuring no accounts are held by individuals or entities listed on the UNSC's Taliban Sanctions List, which has been updated with 17 amended entries as per UNSC press release SC/16352 dated April 28, 2026. Entities must follow the procedures outlined in the RBI's KYC Directions, 2025 and the UAPA Order dated February 2, 2021 (amended April 22, 2024) for account screening and de-listing requests, which should be forwarded to MHA's Joint Secretary (CTCR). Updated sanctions lists for ISIL, Al-Qaida, and Taliban are available on the UN website, and meticulous compliance with these UNSC communications is mandatory for all regulated financial institutions.

# RBI Urban Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025 Summary

These Directions, effective immediately, establish comprehensive regulatory requirements for Urban Co-operative Banks covering board governance, depositor education and awareness fund management, operational compliance, and financial conduct standards. Key requirements include mandatory Board-approved policies for mandatory leave, transfer of unclaimed/inoperative deposits (10+ years) to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, restrictions on prize chit schemes and lottery ticket sales, and prohibitions on accepting deposits from private financiers. The Directions consolidate multiple regulatory aspects including KYC updation procedures, currency futures participation guidelines, mandatory disclosure requirements, and provisions for financial restructuring, strengthening RBI's supervisory framework over the urban co-operative banking sector.

These Master Directions consolidate RBI's requirements for entities seeking membership in centralized payment systems (RTGS, NEFT) and decentralized systems (CTS, ECCS), establishing separate access criteria for each category while ensuring safety and integrity of payment services. All scheduled/licensed banks are eligible for full Type A membership in centralized systems, while Primary Dealers are restricted to Type B membership covering inter-bank and own account transfers, and unlicensed banks may participate only as sub-members in decentralized systems. The directions establish minimum standards for applicants and provide a unified framework replacing previous circulars, with co-operative societies explicitly excluded from direct or sub-membership participation in any payment system.

These Amendment Directions modify Urban Cooperative Banks' income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning norms for stressed asset resolution, effective July 1, 2026. Key requirements include: upgrading NPA accounts to 'Standard' status upon implementation of approved resolution plans, maintaining 5% additional specific provisioning (reversible upon 20% repayment without re-default), and recognizing interest income on accrual basis for resolved accounts. The amendments align with the RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions 2025, enabling banks to provide relief while maintaining prudential standards and promoting sustainable debt resolution through structured restructuring frameworks.

This amendment circular, effective April 1, 2027, aligns the Commercial Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025 with the newly issued Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions, 2026 by updating references to asset classification, NPA determination for project finance, and risk weight calculations. Key modifications include: paragraphs 25(1) and 84 now reference the 2026 asset classification framework; paragraph 132 incorporates the 2026 capital charge standards; and paragraph 172(3)(ii) is deleted for regulatory streamlining. Banks must ensure compliance with the updated asset classification and provisioning requirements under the 2026 directions for loan assets, project finance accounts, and credit risk exposures from the implementation date.

# RBI Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management Directions, 2025

The RBI has issued comprehensive master directions applicable to Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) establishing statutory and regulatory requirements for managing credit risk, including board-approved policies, restrictions on exposures, credit administration procedures, and mandatory use of Legal Entity Identifiers for borrowers. The directions define key credit products (cash credit, current accounts, bills purchased/discounted, bank guarantees) and establish prudential tools to mitigate systemic risks arising from UCBs' interconnected exposures across varied sectors and borrower types. These binding directions become effective immediately and replace previous guidelines, requiring UCBs to strengthen their credit risk management frameworks across statutory restrictions, regulatory limitations, valuation standards, and security filing requirements.

# RBI Directions on Government Pension Disbursement by Agency Banks (2026)

The RBI has issued master directions applicable to all authorized agency banks (PSBs, private banks, payments banks, and small finance banks) for seamless disbursement of Central and State Government pensions, effective immediately from April 30, 2026. Agency banks must promptly implement all government orders regarding pensions (including dearness relief) by directly accessing government websites without waiting for RBI forwarding, and credit pension amounts to pensioner accounts based on Pension Sanctioning Authority orders. The directions establish clear protocols for refunding excess pension payments due to bank errors (credited immediately to government accounts), managing life certificates through digital Jeevan Pramaan service, and ensuring customer service standards including timely pension credits, compensation for delays, sympathetic treatment of elderly/disabled pensioners, and appointment of nodal officers for grievance redressal.

# RBI Local Area Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025

Local Area Banks must obtain RBI prior approval before launching transactional digital banking facilities and must intimate the central bank of view-only facility launches within 30 days along with a Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy Report; all banks must implement comprehensive policies covering statutory and regulatory requirements including liquidity and operational risk management. Eligible banks must have implemented Core Banking Solution and enabled IPv6 traffic handling on their public-facing IT infrastructure to provide either view-only or transactional digital banking services across internet banking, mobile banking, and other digital channels effective January 1, 2026. The directions establish prudential requirements and technological standards to ensure secure digital banking operations while classifying services as either view-only (balance enquiries, statements) or transactional (funds transfers, loans) with varying authorization levels.

These RBI Directions, 2025 establish a comprehensive framework for All India Financial Institutions (EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, and NaBFID) to identify, report, and resolve stressed assets in a time-bound manner through structured resolution plans including restructuring, compromise settlements, and technical write-offs. The Directions mandate board-approved policies for early stress identification, inter-creditor agreements, and specify prudential norms for asset classification, provisioning, and income recognition post-restructuring, with additional provisions for special cases like sale-leaseback transactions and fraudulent borrowers. The framework also establishes regulatory principles for AIFIs' participation in Government Debt Relief Schemes to address credit discipline concerns and moral hazard, while providing exemptions from certain RBI and SEBI regulations to facilitate resolution processes.

The RBI's 2026 Directions introduce a forward-looking Expected Credit Loss (ECL) framework for asset classification and provisioning in commercial banks, effective April 1, 2027, replacing the previous 2025 directions while retaining existing NPA classification norms. Banks must adopt ECL-based provisioning using the Effective Interest Rate method, implement comprehensive model risk management with risk-based tiering, and establish staging frameworks for credit risk assessment. The framework strengthens credit resilience, enhances regulatory transparency, and aligns Indian banking practices with internationally accepted financial reporting standards while requiring extensive disclosures on provisioning methodologies and model validation processes.

# RBI Regulatory Document Summary

The RBI issued comprehensive Responsible Business Conduct Directions for Urban Co-operative Banks effective November 28, 2025, establishing mandatory standards across institutional framework, customer service, financial inclusion, payment services, responsible lending, and deposit management. Key requirements include maintaining transparent disclosure practices, implementing customer protection mechanisms, ensuring accessibility for underserved populations, and adhering to responsible lending conduct standards with specific formulations for Annual Percentage Rate calculations. The Directions apply to all Primary Co-operative Banks classified as UCBs under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, with compliance necessary across ten substantive chapters supported by detailed annexures for operational procedures including claim settlement forms, safe deposit locker inventories, and Key Facts Statements.

# RBI Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025 Summary

These directions, effective January 1, 2026, establish regulatory requirements for commercial banks to offer digital banking services through internet banking, mobile banking, and other digital channels, categorized into view-only facilities (balance inquiries, statements) and transactional facilities (fund transfers, loans). Banks must implement Core Banking Solutions with IPv6-enabled infrastructure, establish comprehensive digital banking policies covering statutory and risk management requirements, and obtain RBI prior approval before launching transactional facilities, with view-only facilities requiring notification within 30 days of launch along with Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy reports. The directions aim to standardize digital banking operations, enhance cybersecurity and operational resilience, and ensure prudential oversight of technology-driven banking services across the sector.

# RBI Payments Banks Debit Card Directions 2025

These Directions establish comprehensive regulatory requirements for payments banks issuing debit cards, including board-approved policies covering issuance, co-branding arrangements, card blocking procedures, and grievance redressal frameworks. Payments banks must issue debit cards only to customers with Savings Bank/Current Accounts without forcing adoption or linking it to other services, and must conduct half-yearly operational reviews including usage analysis. The Directions permit issuance of alternative form factors (wearables, virtual cards) with explicit customer consent, subject to the same prudential and cybersecurity guidelines applicable to physical debit cards.

The RBI has amended paragraph 115 of the Rural Co-operative Banks Investment Portfolio Directions 2025 to simplify the Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR) requirements, now mandating that RCBs maintain a minimum IFR of 5 percent of their investment portfolio classified under the Current Category, assessed annually based on book value as of the balance sheet date. This amendment addresses operational constraints faced by rural cooperative banks in maintaining the reserve by clarifying the calculation methodology and assessment frequency. The amended directions came into effect immediately upon issuance on May 18, 2026, and apply to all Rural Cooperative Banks under RBI's regulatory oversight.

The RBI's Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services Directions, 2025 establish a comprehensive regulatory framework governing financial services expansion for various NBFC categories, including deposit-taking NBFCs, investment companies, factors, microfinance institutions, and housing finance companies, with differentiated requirements based on entity type and operational layers. Key provisions address overseas investments, insurance business entry, mutual fund distribution, money transfer services, pension fund operations, and infrastructure debt fund activities, with specific applicability rules tailored to each NBFC category's risk profile and public interface. The directions empower the RBI to regulate and monitor NBFC diversification into financial services while maintaining prudential standards and consumer protection, with immediate enforcement of the framework across all applicable entities.

The RBI's Second Amendment Directions 2026 modify credit risk management requirements for commercial banks, primarily strengthening Unhedged Foreign Currency Exposure (UFCE) assessment by requiring banks to maintain incremental capital requirements based on potential loss-to-EBID ratios, with a 25 percentage point risk weight increase applied only when exposure exceeds 75 percent. Banks must calculate these incremental capital requirements on a quarterly basis at minimum, using either actual data or conservative projections for new entities, and must apply these requirements over existing credit risk weights under standardized approach guidelines. Additionally, the amendment simplifies country classification procedures by allowing banks to use ECGC's seven-category classification system and mandates quarterly updates, while modifying working capital loan repayment provisions to allow installment or bullet repayment flexibility within prescribed asset classification guidelines.

These Directions establish a framework for Local Area Banks to identify, report, and resolve stressed assets within defined timelines, while rationalizing procedures for compromise settlements and technical write-offs to facilitate asset recovery. LABs participating in State Government Debt Relief Schemes must follow RBI-specified prudential norms and operating procedures to mitigate credit discipline risks and moral hazard concerns arising from debt waivers. The Directions define key terms including "default" (non-payment of debt obligations), "compromise settlement" (negotiated cash settlement with potential sacrifice), and "technical write-off" (accounting adjustments without waiver of recovery rights), and apply immediately to all Local Area Banks.

# Master Direction on Counterfeit Notes, 2023 Summary

Banks must examine all banknotes for authenticity using machines before issuing over counters, feeding ATMs, or remitting to RBI, and must impound detected counterfeit notes with a "COUNTERFEIT NOTE" stamp while issuing acknowledgement receipts to tenders—no counterfeit notes may be returned, destroyed, or credited to accounts. Banks must establish Forged Notes Vigilance Cells at head offices with designated nodal officers to report counterfeit detections to police: consolidated monthly reports for up to four pieces per transaction, and immediate FIR filings for five or more pieces, with copies sent to both police and the bank's vigilance cell. Failure to impound counterfeit notes will be treated as willful involvement in circulating counterfeit currency and subject to penalty, with banks required to maintain detailed records and provide monthly data reports to RBI and government authorities.

# RBI Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rates on Advances Directions, 2025

Rural Co-operative Banks must determine lending rates transparently with Board approval, considering cost of funds and transaction costs, while charging interest at monthly rests (except for agricultural advances linked to crop seasons). Banks must publish minimum and maximum interest rates in all branches and establish Board-approved policies for microfinance loans that document interest rate models with clearly delineated cost components (funds, risk premium, margin) based on objective parameters. For small-value loans, banks must implement prior-approval processes considering borrower cash flows, incorporate justified risk premiums based on borrower ratings, ensure total borrowing costs are justifiable, and fix appropriate ceilings on interest and charges.

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 regulate the establishment and operation of banking outlets, digital banking units, and alternative service delivery channels by commercial banks in India, effective immediately. The directions require banks to obtain board-approved policies for branch authorization and establish robust governance frameworks for managing various banking outlets including branches, ATMs, digital banking units, business correspondents, and doorstep banking services. Banks must comply with specific infrastructure, cybersecurity, customer grievance redressal, and reporting requirements while foreign banks operating in branch mode face separate regulatory provisions.

Banks must report all currency chest transactions on the same day by 9 PM through ICCOMS to link offices, which must consolidate and report to Issue Offices by 11 PM, with penal interest levied on T+0 basis for any delays or wrong reporting. Penal interest is charged until corrected advice is received, and soiled note remittances wrongly reported as withdrawals incur a fixed penalty of Rs. 50,000 regardless of amount or duration. The Master Direction ensures discipline in timely and accurate reporting of currency chest transactions under RBI's Clean Note Policy, with no maximum cap on penal interest to incentivize compliance.

The RBI has amended the Local Area Banks Credit Risk Management Directions by inserting Chapter IIA on Credit Risk Evaluation, requiring banks to factor calamities' potential impact on borrowers into their credit assessments. This amendment is issued under sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and becomes effective July 1, 2026. The directive aims to strengthen credit risk management practices by ensuring LABs consider disaster-related vulnerabilities when evaluating borrower creditworthiness.

The RBI Master Directions on Small Finance Banks – Credit Facilities (2025, updated April 2026) establish comprehensive regulatory frameworks governing credit products including digital lending, gold-collateral loans, microfinance, project finance, real estate lending, infrastructure financing, and export credit. The Directions mandate that Small Finance Banks implement robust board oversight, customer protection mechanisms, technology safeguards, and prudential conditions across all lending categories while ensuring compliance with loan-to-value ratios, income assessment protocols, and credit information reporting requirements. These regulations aim to balance financial innovation and credit growth with systemic stability, depositor protection, and borrower safeguards through clearly defined eligibility criteria, appraisal standards, and monitoring protocols for each lending category.

Small Finance Banks must maintain an Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR) of at least 2% of their Available-for-Sale (AFS) and Fair Value Through Profit or Loss (FVTPL) portfolio, assessed annually on balance sheet dates. IFR contributions shall be made from realized gains on investment sales and net profit after mandatory appropriations, addressing operational constraints faced by banks under the previous framework. This amendment, effective immediately from May 18, 2026, provides operational flexibility while maintaining prudential standards for investment portfolio management.

The RBI (Housing Finance Companies) Directions, 2025 (updated April 15, 2026) establish comprehensive regulatory requirements for all registered HFCs under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, covering capital adequacy, asset classification, provisioning, public deposit acceptance, corporate governance, and fair practices. Key requirements include mandatory compliance with prudential norms on capital, regulatory restrictions on lending limits, governance standards for board oversight and auditor independence, and submission of regulatory reports, with HFCs also subject to applicable provisions of parallel NBFC directions where non-contradictory. The directions aim to prevent HFCs from conducting affairs detrimentally to investors' and depositors' interests while enabling the RBI to regulate the financial system effectively through a framework that categorizes HFCs into different regulatory layers with scale-based obligations.

Banks maintaining currency chests must report all transactions through ICCOMS by 9 PM the same day, with link offices consolidating and reporting to Issue Offices by 11 PM, subject to penal interest levies for delays, wrong reporting, or non-reporting. Penal interest is calculated on a T+0 basis (from the transaction date) and applies to all cases of incorrect Link Office Statement reporting regardless of correct chest slip submission, with a fixed ₹50,000 penalty for wrongly reporting soiled note remittances as withdrawals. The RBI enforces these strict reporting disciplines to maintain the Clean Note Policy, with no maximum cap on penal interest recovery to ensure sustained compliance and accurate currency management across the banking system.

These Directions, effective January 1, 2026, establish regulatory requirements for Rural Co-operative Banks (State and Central Co-operative Banks) to offer digital banking channels including internet banking, mobile banking, and other digital services through view-only and transactional facilities. Banks must implement Core Banking Solution (CBS) and IPv6-enabled IT infrastructure, establish comprehensive policies covering statutory/regulatory requirements, and submit Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy (GAICA) reports to RBI's DOR within thirty days of board approval to launch digital services. The framework sets prudential standards and technological guidelines to ensure secure, compliant digital banking operations while managing operational and liquidity risks in rural co-operative banking sector.

The Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 establish comprehensive capital adequacy and risk-weighted asset (RWA) calculation requirements applicable to all Local Area Banks in India, effective immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025. The directions mandate minimum regulatory capital norms with detailed specifications for Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital composition, deductions, cross-holding limits, and subsidiary capital requirements to ensure financial stability. LABs must calculate capital ratios based on standardized RWA methodologies covering credit risk, market risk, and interest rate derivatives, with strict reporting requirements for investments by FIIs and NRIs in qualifying capital instruments.

These Directions establish mandatory financial statement presentation and disclosure requirements for Urban Co-operative Banks (classified as Level-I enterprises) under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, requiring compliance with all applicable Accounting Standards issued by ICAI. Banks must prepare Balance Sheets and Profit & Loss Accounts in the formats specified in the Third Schedule of the BR Act, 1949, and follow RBI guidelines on accounting treatments including provisions for fraud, nostro account reconciliation, and deferred tax liabilities. The Directions apply to all Primary Co-operative Banks and came into effect upon placement on the RBI website, superseding previous versions and ensuring uniform financial reporting standards across the urban cooperative banking sector.

The RBI issued the Small Finance Banks (Governance) Directions, 2025, effective immediately, establishing comprehensive governance requirements for all Small Finance Banks, including mandatory board structures with Independent Directors and key committees (Audit, Risk Management, Nomination and Remuneration). The Directions mandate specific provisions for appointment and remuneration of senior management (MD&CEO, CFO, CRO) with fit-and-proper criteria, clawback mechanisms, and malus arrangements for variable pay, while non-scheduled SFBs are exempted from certain provisions regarding CRO, CFO, and CTO appointments. These governance standards apply to all SFBs notwithstanding prior RBI notifications, though existing Directors in converting entities retain grandfathered terms until their appointment completion.

# RBI Circular Summary: Urban Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management Directions, 2025

These Directions, effective immediately, establish consolidated prudential exposure limits for Urban Co-operative Banks to manage concentration risk by restricting exposures to individual borrowers and connected groups based on Tier-I Capital, thereby preventing excessive reliance on large borrowers or interconnected counterparties. The Directions define credit exposure (including loans, non-funded limits, and commitments), investment exposure in non-SLR securities, and group definitions based on commonality of management and control, with provisions allowing banks discretion in grouping decisions based on available information. UCBs must comply with specified exposure norms for individual borrowers, borrower groups, unsecured advances, inter-bank exposures, and small-value loans, consolidating previously issued prudential norms under a single regulatory framework to ensure granular portfolio distribution and mitigate asset-side concentration risks.

# RBI Payments Banks Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025 Summary

The Reserve Bank of India has issued new master directions effective immediately to regulate branch authorization and banking outlet operations for payments banks under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, establishing comprehensive governance requirements for the board of directors and standardized policies for branch expansion. Payments banks must comply with definitions and operational standards for various banking outlets (branches, extension counters, satellite offices, part-time outlets), which must deliver services minimum four hours daily for five days weekly, while administrative offices and back offices are explicitly prohibited from direct customer interface. The directions establish detailed requirements for business facilitators, business correspondents, and doorstep banking services, including eligibility criteria, risk management protocols, information reporting obligations, and grievance redressal mechanisms to ensure consumer protection and regulatory oversight.

These Directions establish Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements for Urban Co-operative Banks in India, effective immediately, requiring them to maintain specified reserves and report compliance through designated statutory returns (Form B for scheduled banks and Form I for non-scheduled banks). Banks must apportion savings bank deposits into demand and time liabilities using a standardized half-yearly calculation method, and maintain SLR in the form of approved securities including dated Government of India securities, Treasury Bills, and State Development Loans, with only unencumbered portions qualifying as specified SLR assets. Non-compliance with these reserve maintenance requirements may result in penalties as outlined in Chapter VI, and banks must submit regular reporting under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

Urban Cooperative Banks must maintain a minimum Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR) of 5 percent of their investment portfolio (calculated on book value of HFT and AFS category investments as of balance sheet date), assessed annually, with discretion to maintain higher percentages based on portfolio size and composition with Board approval. Banks may now draw down IFR balances in excess of 5 percent for credit to profit/loss accounts at year-end, addressing operational constraints faced by UCBs in maintaining the reserve. These amendments to the 2025 Directions became effective immediately upon issuance on May 18, 2026, providing UCBs greater flexibility in IFR management while maintaining prudential minimum requirements.

The Master Direction consolidates RBI's regulations on miscellaneous remittance facilities for residents under FEMA 1999, permitting various current account transactions such as travel allowances, salary remittances, medical expense payments for NRI relatives, and international card usage through authorized dealers. Authorized dealers must comply with the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules 2000, which explicitly prohibit certain transactions (Schedule I), require government approvals for others (Schedule II), and delegate authority to dealers for transactions within specified limits (Schedule III). The directive establishes operational guidelines for authorized persons to conduct foreign exchange business with customers while implementing regulatory frameworks, with provisions for income tax clearance requirements and reporting through designated master directions.

These Directions establish interest rate guidelines for Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) effective immediately, permitting banks to determine lending rates based on cost of funds and transaction costs with Board approval, while requiring transparent disclosure of minimum and maximum rates at all branches. Banks must charge interest on advances at monthly rests, except for agricultural advances which follow crop-season-based practices, and implement Board-approved policies incorporating risk premiums, cost justification, and appropriate ceilings, particularly for small value loans and microfinance. The framework emphasizes that while rates are deregulated, UCBs must avoid usurious practices, ensure fair pricing aligned with banking norms, and apply specific safeguards for vulnerable borrowers including small and marginal farmers.

Regional Rural Banks must create an Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR) from realized gains on investment sales, subject to net profit availability, with a minimum requirement of 2% of their HFT and AFS portfolio. The minimum IFR requirement is to be assessed annually based on the book value of investments in AFS and HFT categories as of the balance sheet date. This amendment, effective immediately from May 18, 2026, addresses operational constraints faced by RRBs in maintaining the IFR under previous directions.

# RBI Master Direction Summary

Foreign entities seeking to establish branch offices, liaison offices, or project offices in India must obtain prior Reserve Bank of India (RBI) approval through Authorized Dealer Category-I banks, with applications processed in consultation with the Government of India for sensitive cases including applicants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Iran, China, Hong Kong, Macau (in restricted regions), and those in defence, telecom, private security, and information/broadcasting sectors. The Master Direction consolidates existing instructions on establishment procedures, permissible activities, bank account opening, annual compliance certifications, profit remittance, and office closure, with specific provisions for extension of validity periods and additional activities. Authorized Dealer banks must ensure foreign entities comply with registration requirements, submit annual activity certificates, and follow prescribed formats including the Letter of Comfort and Form FNC for regulatory oversight and reporting purposes.

# RBI Amendment Directions on Credit Risk Transfer - Summary

The RBI has amended the Commercial Banks Credit Risk Transfer Directions 2025 to align acquired loan recognition and measurement with the Asset Classification Directions 2026, requiring permitted transferees to follow standardized accounting treatment. Stressed loans acquired by banks must now be classified as Purchased or Originated Credit-Impaired (POCI) assets with provisioning and measurement guided by POCI guidelines, replacing previous separate treatment provisions. When banks transfer stressed loans to Asset Reconstruction Companies at prices below net book value, the resulting shortfall must be immediately debited to the profit and loss account, effective from April 1, 2027.

The Master Direction (updated October 1, 2024) establishes the RBI's framework for compounding FEMA 1999 contraventions, which allows individuals and entities to settle violations through a streamlined process rather than formal prosecution, except for Section 3(a) violations. Compounding authority is tiered by contravention amount: Assistant General Manager (up to Rs 10 lakh), Deputy General Manager (Rs 10-40 lakh), General Manager (Rs 40-100 lakh), and Chief General Manager (Rs 100 lakh and above), with applications processed within 180 days. AD Category-I and Authorised banks must inform constituents of this mechanism and comply with reporting requirements, enabling efficient resolution of foreign exchange violations while maintaining regulatory oversight.

The RBI has amended the NBFC regulatory framework effective July 1, 2026, introducing new "Type I NBFC" and "Unregistered Type I NBFC" categories for entities not accepting public funds and lacking customer interface. NBFCs in these categories with asset size below ₹1,000 crore are exempted from RBI registration requirements under sections 45IA and 45IC, with existing registered entities permitted to apply for deregistration by December 31, 2026. The amendment clarifies definitions of public funds and customer interface, including indirect receipt of funds through associates and group entities, while providing a standardized regulatory classification framework for scale-based regulation of non-banking financial companies.

The RBI has issued the Payments Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025, effective immediately, establishing comprehensive framework requirements for managing liquidity and interest rate risks at payments banks. Payments banks must implement robust governance structures with board oversight, maintain detailed liquidity risk management policies covering flow and stock approaches, stress testing, and contingency funding plans, while also managing interest rate risk through both earnings and economic value perspectives. Banks are required to prepare and submit regular regulatory returns on liquidity and interest rate risk positions, maintain diversified funding strategies, and establish internal controls and management information systems to monitor these risks across all currencies and intraday periods.

Payments Banks with 10 or more banking outlets as of March 31, 2025, must establish an Internal Ombudsman (IO) position, with the IO being a retired or serving officer at General Manager level or equivalent with minimum seven years of relevant experience in financial sector areas. The Directions strengthen internal grievance redress mechanisms by enabling apex-level review of rejected customer complaints before final rejection, ensuring speedy resolution of deficiency in service matters. Most provisions are effective immediately, except specific clauses requiring compliance by June 30, 2026, with the RBI retaining authority to suspend or extend applicability as deemed necessary.
